title: Choosing materials: no material is best, so how do we choose?

summary.text: A strip of paper bends easily. Dried flour paste snaps like a biscuit. But glue four layers of paper together with that paste, and the bar holds more than either one alone. Your child makes these bars and loads them until they fail, to find out how two weak things can make a strong one. Then they take up a harder question: if no material is best at everything, how do we choose? They score materials for a job, follow a thing from the ground to the bin, and bury scraps in soil to see which ones rot.
summary.art: A kitchen table with four dried bars of paper and paste laid across two piles of books, a hanging cup of water on one bar, and a jar of soil with scraps in it beside a notebook with a scoring table.

intro.hook: A steel tumbler never breaks, but it is heavy and it gets too hot to hold. A paper cup is light and cheap, but it goes soft and you throw it away. A clay cup keeps water cool, but it can crack. A plastic cup is light and tough, but it may stay in the ground for hundreds of years. Which cup is the best cup?
intro.text: There is no best cup. Each one wins at something and loses at something else. In the Class 3 unit you matched properties to jobs, one job at a time. But a real job needs many things at once, and getting more of one often means getting less of another. In this unit you will score materials for a job, see why mixing two weak materials can make a strong one, and follow a thing from where it comes from to where it goes. Then you will bury scraps in soil and see which ones rot.
intro.art: Four cups on a kitchen table in a row, steel, paper, clay and plastic, each with a small tag that says what it is good at and what it is bad at.

outcomes: I can list what a job needs, score two or more materials against it, and say why the best choice can change when the job or the place changes.
I can explain what a composite is, and why two weak materials joined together can give a strong one.
I can explain what an alloy is, and why mixing metals can make them harder.
I can follow one object through its whole life, from its source to what happens after, and say what each stage costs.
I can tell the difference between a material that rots, one that can be made again and one that lasts for a very long time.
I can work out the cost of an object for each year or each use, and say why the cheapest to buy is not always the cheapest to own.
I can say what I do not know yet about a choice, and which test or fact I would need to find out.

terms.meaning: One thing a job needs from a material, such as strong, light, cheap or waterproof. A job usually has many requirements at once.
terms.example: A school bag must be light, strong, waterproof and cheap. Those are four requirements.
terms.art: A school bag with four labels pointing to it: light, strong, waterproof, cheap.

terms.meaning: When getting more of one good thing means getting less of another. Every material choice is a trade-off.
terms.example: A thicker steel plate is stronger but heavier. A thinner plate is lighter but weaker.
terms.art: A balance with strong on one side and light on the other, tipping toward strong.

terms.meaning: A table that scores each material on each requirement, so you can compare them side by side. The rows are materials and the columns are requirements.
terms.example: A table that scores steel, plastic and glass for a lunch box on cost, weight and safety.
terms.art: A table on paper with materials down the side, requirements along the top and numbers in the boxes.

terms.meaning: A number that says how much a requirement matters for this job. A requirement that matters more gets a bigger weight.
terms.example: For a hot-day water bottle, keeping water cool gets a weight of 3 and looks gets a weight of 1.
terms.art: Three stones of different sizes labelled with weights 3, 2 and 1.

terms.meaning: A number you give a material for one requirement. A higher score means it does better.
terms.example: Steel scores 5 for strong and 2 for light.
terms.art: A row of a table with a 5 and a 2 circled in different colours.

terms.meaning: A material made of two or more different materials joined together, so that the result can do what neither could do alone.
terms.example: Mud mixed with straw makes a brick that does not crack as easily as mud alone.
terms.art: A cross-section of a mud brick with straw fibres running through it.

terms.meaning: A very thin thread. In a composite, the fibres usually carry the pull. Straw, paper, cotton and glass fibre are examples.
terms.example: The paper layers in a papier-mâché bar are fibres.
terms.art: A bundle of thin threads lying in a row, with an arrow pulling at both ends.

terms.meaning: The material that holds the fibres in place and passes the load from one fibre to the next. It is often a glue, a paste, mud or plastic.
terms.example: Flour paste is the matrix in a paper and paste bar.
terms.art: A rectangle of paste with paper fibres lying inside it like threads in jelly.

terms.meaning: A metal made by mixing two or more metals, or a metal and another element, such as carbon. An alloy is often harder than the metals it is made from.
terms.example: Brass is copper mixed with zinc. Steel is iron mixed with a little carbon.
terms.art: A pot of melted metal with two coloured streams being poured in, and a solid bar of the mixed metal beside it.

terms.meaning: The whole life of an object: where its material comes from, how it is made, how it is used and what happens after.
terms.example: A steel katori begins as iron ore in the ground and ends as scrap that can be melted again.
terms.art: A circle of four pictures joined by arrows: ground, factory, kitchen, scrapyard.

terms.meaning: Where a material first comes from, such as a tree, a field, the ground or a factory.
terms.example: The source of cotton is a plant. The source of plastic is oil or gas from the ground.
terms.art: A cotton plant and an oil well in two separate pictures, each with a label.

terms.meaning: A source that can grow back or be refilled in a person's lifetime, such as cotton, wood or bamboo.
terms.example: Bamboo can grow tall again within a few years after it is cut.
terms.art: A bamboo grove with a cut stump and a tall new shoot beside it.

terms.meaning: A source that cannot be replaced within a human lifetime, such as oil, coal or metal ore.
terms.example: Oil took millions of years to form. We use it up far faster than it forms.
terms.art: An oil drop beside a long calendar of millions of years.

terms.meaning: Able to be broken down by living things such as bacteria and fungi, and turned back into soil.
terms.example: A banana peel is biodegradable. A steel spoon is not.
terms.art: A banana peel turning into brown soil over four small pictures.

terms.meaning: Dark, crumbly soil made when tiny living things break down plant and food waste. It feeds new plants.
terms.example: Vegetable peels in a pot of soil turn into compost in a few weeks.
terms.art: A pot of dark crumbly compost with a small green seedling in the soil.

terms.meaning: To break a used material down and make it into new things. Steel, glass, aluminium and paper can be recycled.
terms.example: Old newspapers are soaked and made into new paper.
terms.art: Old newspapers going into a tub of water and coming out as a sheet of new paper.

terms.meaning: To use a thing again for the same job or a new job, without breaking it down first.
terms.example: A glass jar that held pickle is reused to hold rice.
terms.art: A pickle jar on a shelf filled with dry rice.

terms.meaning: To mend a thing instead of throwing it away. Repair uses less new material than making a new thing.
terms.example: A torn bag mended with a patch and thread is repaired.
terms.art: A needle and thread stitching a cloth patch on a torn bag.

terms.meaning: A big pit or heap where rubbish is buried. Things that do not rot stay there for a very long time.
terms.example: Plastic bags that are not recycled often end up in a landfill.
terms.art: A cross-section of a landfill with layers of rubbish and soil, and a plastic bag intact deep in the heap.

terms.meaning: The slow eating away of a metal by air and water. Rust is the corrosion of iron and steel.
terms.example: A steel pin left in a damp place turns orange.
terms.art: An iron nail with orange rust on one half and bright metal on the other.

terms.meaning: All the energy used to make a thing, from digging up the material to bringing it to the shop.
terms.example: Making a new aluminium can from ore takes far more energy than making one from old cans.
terms.art: A can with a ribbon of small sun symbols winding from a mine, to a factory, to a shop.

terms.meaning: The price of a thing divided by the number of times you use it. It is a fairer way to compare a cheap thing that breaks with an expensive thing that lasts.
terms.example: A cloth bag costs 40 rupees and is used 200 times. The cost per use is 20 paise.
terms.art: A price tag of 40 rupees divided by a row of 200 tick marks.

terms.meaning: A tiny piece of plastic, smaller than a grain of rice. Big plastic things break into microplastics over many years, and the pieces get into water, soil and living bodies.
terms.example: A polyester shirt sheds tiny threads in the wash, and the threads are microplastics.
terms.art: A magnified drop of water with tiny coloured plastic specks floating in it.

terms.meaning: Three sentences. The claim says what you think is true. The evidence says what you saw. The reasoning says why the evidence supports the claim.
terms.example: Claim: layered paper and paste is stronger. Evidence: the bar held three times the water. Reasoning: the paper carries the pull and the paste joins the layers.
terms.art: A notebook with three lines, marked by a speech bubble, an eye and a lightbulb.

explanations.concept: There is no best material, only trade-offs
explanations.definition: A trade-off means that getting more of one good thing costs you some of another. Every material choice has one.
explanations.description: Think about a drinking cup. Steel does not break and lasts for years, but it is heavy, it gets too hot to hold, and it costs more. Glass is clear and does not change the taste, but it breaks. Paper is light and cheap, but it goes soft and is used once. Clay keeps water cool, but it cracks if it falls. Plastic is light and tough, but it can last in the ground for a very long time. Each one wins in some ways and loses in others. This is a trade-off: to get more of one good thing, you give up some of another. Because every material has a catch, choosing is a skill. First, you decide what the job needs. Then you decide which needs matter most. Only then can you pick the material that gives up the least of what matters.
examples: A steel tumbler is strong but heavy and hot to hold. A paper cup is light but weak.
A thick glass bottle does not leak, but it breaks if dropped. A plastic bottle does not break if dropped, but it may leak.
A bicycle frame of thin steel tube is light and strong, but costs more than a heavy frame.
explanations.art: Five cups in a row, steel, glass, paper, clay and plastic, each with two small icons showing one thing it is good at and one thing it is bad at.
explanations.context: A steel cup, a paper cup, a clay cup and a plastic cup each have a weak side. This card explains why no material is best at everything, and what that means for choosing.

explanations.concept: A decision matrix: scoring materials for a job
explanations.definition: A decision matrix is a table that scores each material against each need, using weights for how much each need matters.
explanations.description: When a job has many needs, a table helps you compare. Put the materials down the side and the needs along the top. Give each need a weight from 1 to 3 for how much it matters. Then give each material a score from 1 to 5 for each need. Multiply each score by the weight and add up the row. The highest total is the best fit for this job. Suppose you want a tiffin box for school. 'Cost' has weight 2, 'light' has weight 2, 'does not leak' has weight 3 and 'lasts' has weight 1. A plastic box might score 4 on cost, 5 on light, 3 on leaks and 3 on lasting. A steel box might score 2, 3, 5 and 5. Multiply each score by its weight and add up each row to get the totals. But be honest: the scores are your judgement, not facts. Change the weights and the winner may change. That is useful, because it shows what people are really disagreeing about.
examples: Plastic: 4 times 2, plus 5 times 2, plus 3 times 3, plus 3 times 1, which is 30.
Steel: 2 times 2, plus 3 times 2, plus 5 times 3, plus 5 times 1, which is 30. It is a tie, and the weights decide.
If the box will carry curry in a school bag, the weight for 'does not leak' goes up and steel wins.
explanations.art: A table on paper with four rows for materials and four columns for needs, numbers in each box and a total on the right, with one total circled.
explanations.context: Choosing by feeling can be unfair. This card shows how a table of scores helps you compare materials on many needs at once.

explanations.concept: The same job in a different place needs a different material
explanations.definition: The best material for a job depends on the place, the people and the price, as well as the job.
explanations.description: In Chennai in May, a school water bottle must keep water cool and survive a hot bag. In Leh in January, water in a bottle freezes, so the bottle must not crack when the water expands. A house in Cherrapunji, where the monsoon is very heavy, needs roofs that shed water and walls that dry. A house in the Thar desert needs thick walls that keep out the midday heat. The job looks the same on paper, but the place changes what matters. So does the price people can pay, and the materials near them. Mud and straw are free in a village. Steel and glass are cheaper in a city with a factory. A good engineer asks, 'where?' and 'for whom?' before asking 'which material?'. A choice that is smart in one place can be foolish in another.
examples: Thick mud walls keep the Thar desert's afternoon heat out of a house.
Roofs in rainy Kerala and Meghalaya are sloped to shed water quickly.
A thick down jacket is a good choice in Leh in January and a bad choice in Chennai in May.
explanations.art: Three houses side by side: a mud house with thick walls in a desert, a sloping tiled roof house in a rainy hill village and a stone house with small windows in a cold mountain town.
explanations.context: The same job can ask for a different material in a different place. This card explains how place, people and price change the choice.

explanations.concept: Composites: two weak things that make a strong one
explanations.definition: A composite is a material made of two or more materials joined so that the result can do what neither could do alone.
explanations.description: A composite is a material made of two or more different materials joined together. Usually one is a fibre and the other is a matrix. The fibre is a thin thread that is strong when pulled. The matrix is a paste, mud or glue that holds the fibres and shares the load between them. Mud alone cracks, because it is brittle and a crack runs straight through it. Straw alone can be pulled, but it has no shape. Mixed together, the straw stops cracks from running far, and the mud holds the straw in place. The brick is better than either part. Paper and paste work the same way. Concrete is a composite too: stone and cement are strong when squeezed, and steel bars inside carry the pull. Bone is a composite of hard mineral and soft protein. Wood is a composite of long cellulose fibres held by a stiff glue. Nature uses this trick everywhere.
examples: Mud and straw bricks, used in many villages, crack less than plain mud.
Reinforced concrete is stone and cement with steel bars inside. Most big buildings use it.
A fishing boat made of fibreglass is glass fibres held in hard plastic.
explanations.art: A mud brick cut open to show straw fibres inside it, with a crack starting from one side and stopping when it meets a straw fibre.
explanations.context: Mixing two weak materials can give one strong one. This card explains how a composite works, with the fibre and the matrix.

explanations.concept: Alloys: why mixing metals makes them harder
explanations.definition: An alloy is a metal mixed with other atoms. The odd-sized atoms stop the layers of metal from sliding, so the alloy is usually harder.
explanations.description: A pure metal is made of atoms packed in neat layers. When you push hard, the layers slide over each other, so pure copper and pure iron bend easily. An alloy is a metal mixed with other atoms of a different size. The odd-sized atoms get in the way when the layers try to slide, like marbles jammed in a stack of oranges. So the alloy is harder. Bronze is copper mixed with tin. Brass is copper mixed with zinc. Steel is iron mixed with a tiny amount of carbon, often less than two parts in a hundred. Bronze was one of the first alloys people made. The small bronze statue known as the Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro, about 4,500 years old, was made of a copper alloy. In India, bell metal, called kansa, is an alloy of copper and tin used for bells, gongs and dinner plates for centuries.
examples: Brass is harder than pure copper, so it is used for taps, locks and instruments.
Stainless steel has chromium mixed in, which keeps it from rusting.
Bell metal is copper with a good deal of tin, which makes a clear ringing sound.
explanations.art: A stack of oranges sliding easily, and the same stack with a few marbles jammed between the layers so it will not slide, beside a bar of bronze.
explanations.context: Metals are often mixed on purpose. This card explains what an alloy is, and why the mix is harder than the metals alone.

explanations.concept: The whole life of a thing: source, making, use and after
explanations.definition: The life cycle of an object is its whole story: where the material comes from, how it is made, how it is used and what happens after.
explanations.description: Every object has a life. It starts at a source: a cotton field, an iron mine, an oil well. It goes to a factory or workshop where it is made, and this takes energy, water and labour. Then it is used, perhaps for days, perhaps for years. Finally it ends up somewhere: it rots, it is melted and made again, it is burned, or it sits in the ground. Looking at all four stages is called looking at the life cycle. A steel katori starts as iron ore, takes a lot of energy to make, lasts for decades and can be melted and made again. A plastic bag starts as oil or gas, takes little energy to make, lasts a few minutes of use and may stay in the ground for a very long time. A cotton bag starts as a plant, needs water to grow, and rots at the end. The cheapest at the shop is not always the cheapest for the world. Each stage has a cost, even if nobody sends us a bill for it.
examples: A paper bag takes trees and water to make, and it rots in soil in weeks to months.
A cloth bag takes more energy to make than a plastic bag, but it can be used hundreds of times.
A glass bottle is heavy to carry and takes energy to make. It can be washed and refilled, or crushed and melted into a new bottle.
explanations.art: A circle of four pictures joined by arrows: a cotton field, a factory loom, a child carrying a bag, and a heap of old cloth being shredded for compost.
explanations.context: A bag costs a few rupees at the shop, but that is only part of its story. This card explains how to look at the whole life of an object.

explanations.concept: What happens after: rot, rust, remake or stay
explanations.definition: After use, a material may rot, rust, be remade or stay for a very long time. Which one depends on what it is made of.
explanations.description: After we finish with a thing, its material goes one of four ways. Some things rot. Banana leaf, paper, cotton cloth and vegetable peel are food for bacteria and fungi, who break them down into soil. Some things rust. Iron and steel combine slowly with oxygen and water and crumble. Some things can be remade. Steel, aluminium and glass can be melted and made into new things, again and again, without losing their quality. Paper can be pulped and remade a few times, but its fibres get shorter each time, so the paper gets weaker. Some things stay. Most plastics are made of very long, tough molecule chains that bacteria and fungi did not meet until the last hundred years or so, and so they cannot easily break them. Big plastics slowly crack into tiny pieces called microplastics. They get smaller but they do not disappear. A material that cannot rot has to be remade or kept in use, or it piles up.
examples: Banana peel, left in damp soil, rots within weeks.
An aluminium can can be melted and made into a new can again and again.
Experts estimate that a plastic bottle can last for hundreds of years in a landfill. Nobody has watched one for long enough to see it break down fully.
explanations.art: Four paths leaving a pile of used things: one to soil with a seedling, one to a rusty heap, one to a furnace and back to a new can, and one to a long dusty road with tiny specks along it.
explanations.context: Throwing a thing away does not make it vanish. This card explains the four things that can happen to a material after we finish with it.

explanations.concept: Can plastic be eaten? The race against plastic waste
explanations.description: For many years, people thought no living being could break down plastic. In 2016, a team of scientists in Japan led by Shosuke Yoshida reported a bacterium, Ideonella sakaiensis, that they found at a plastic bottle recycling site. She could use the plastic in some bottles, called PET, as food. Her enzymes, the chemicals a living being makes to break things down, cut the plastic's long chains into smaller pieces. Other groups have found enzymes in other microbes, and have improved them in laboratories. Some wax worm caterpillars and some fungi have also been reported to chew some plastics. But the pace is slow, and it is not clear this can solve the waste problem. Many plastics are not PET. Some are mixtures of several plastics. Some have other chemicals added. Scientists disagree about whether enzymes can clean up a landfill, or whether the better answer is to make less plastic, reuse it more and design new plastics that are made to break down. Both sides agree that we do not yet have a simple fix.
examples: Some labs are making enzymes that break PET bottles down into their building blocks in a few days. The building blocks can then be made into new bottles.
Cotton, wool and paper are made by living beings, and living beings can break them down. That is why they rot.
Some new plastics made from plants are designed to break down, but many only do so in hot industrial compost.

perspectives.explanation: Enzymes that break down PET could let us remake bottles from old bottles, so we do not need new oil. We should keep improving them.
Enzymes work only on some plastics, in the right place, at the right heat. The biggest saving is to make and throw away less plastic.
We should design things from the start for their whole life, so that the material rots or can be remade, and no clean-up is needed.

explanations.art: A magnified view of a bacterium cutting a long chain of plastic into small pieces, beside a plastic bottle.
explanations.context: Plastic lasts a very long time. This card is about the discovery of a bacterium that can eat one kind of plastic, and what scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: Old choices, tested by long use
explanations.definition: Old choices of materials were tested by long use. Many have good reasons, and some beliefs about them still need testing.
explanations.description: Before laboratories and plastics, people chose materials by trying them for generations. Many of their choices have good reasons. Banana leaf plates are light, flat, waterproof enough for a meal and rot in a few weeks, so there is nothing to wash and nothing left. Clay pots keep water cool, because a little water seeps through the clay and dries on the outside. Coir ropes and mats are strong, do not rot quickly in salt water and come from a coconut tree that grows again. Mud and lime plaster let a wall breathe. Brass and copper vessels were used for water and cooking for a very long time. Not every old belief is proved. For example, many people believe that water from a copper vessel is healthier. Studies show copper can kill some germs on its surface, but the claims about health are still being debated. A good scientist honours old knowledge and tests it. Some of it turns out to be wise, and some of it does not.
examples: Banana leaf plates and areca leaf plates are made from leaves, and are used in many parts of India.
Coir mats and ropes are made from the husk of coconuts.
A clay kullad is used once and then returns to the earth as clay pieces.
explanations.art: A grandmother in a kitchen serving rice on a banana leaf, with a clay pot of water and a coir mat on the floor beside her.
explanations.context: Long before plastic and factories, people chose materials by trying them for generations. This card explains why many old choices were wise, and why they still need testing.

explanations.concept: The Iron Pillar of Delhi: why has it hardly rusted?
explanations.description: In Delhi, near the Qutub Minar, stands an iron pillar about seven metres tall. It was made more than 1,500 years ago, probably in the Gupta period. It has stood in the open air through monsoons for centuries, and it has not rusted away. Iron usually rusts in months when it is left out in the rain. So what is special about this pillar? One explanation, from R. Balasubramaniam and others at IIT Kanpur, is that the iron has a lot of phosphorus in it, and a thin skin of a phosphorus compound formed on the surface and shielded the iron below. Other scientists have stressed that Delhi's climate is dry for much of the year, so the iron stays dry for months. Others note that the pillar is also protected by the oils and touch of many hands over centuries. Maybe all of these matter. The pillar shows that a good material choice can be a combination of the right material and the right place.
examples: Iron with a lot of phosphorus, like the pillar's, is different from the low-phosphorus iron of most modern steel.
Delhi has a dry climate for most of the year, which slows rusting.
The same pillar in a damp place by the sea, such as Mumbai or Kochi, would probably rust faster.

perspectives.explanation: A thin protective skin containing phosphorus formed on the surface and slowed rusting. The metal itself was made in a special way.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study climate and corrosion
perspectives.explanation: Delhi is dry for much of the year. Iron lasts longer where the air is dry, so the place did a lot of the work.
The history of the pillar, including how people have touched and treated it, matters too. We do not know the whole story.

explanations.art: A tall iron pillar in a courtyard in front of an old stone gateway, with a visitor looking up at it, and a magnified circle showing a thin skin on the surface.
explanations.context: A pillar made of iron has stood in Delhi for about 1,500 years without rusting through. This card explains the ideas about why, and why the question is still open.

explanations.concept: A material's real cost can show up later
explanations.definition: The full cost of a material may show up years after it is used. A test answers only the question it was built to ask.
explanations.description: For a long time, asbestos was a popular material in many countries, including India, for roof sheets and pipes. It does not burn, it is cheap and it is strong. Later, doctors found that tiny asbestos fibres in the lungs could cause serious illness, many years after breathing them in. Lead was added to paint and to petrol because it helped paint last and engines run smoothly. Later, scientists showed that lead harms children's brains, and most countries banned it. In each case, the first tests asked 'does it do the job?' Nobody asked, for years, 'what does it do to bodies, many years later?' A test answers only the question it asks. This is why engineers and doctors now try to look at the whole life, including the long-term effects. It is also why we should be careful with a new material, especially one that will be everywhere.
examples: Asbestos roof sheets were used in India for decades, and many are still on roofs.
Lead in petrol was phased out in India in 2000.
Some chemicals used in non-stick pans have been found in water and blood, and scientists are studying their effects.
explanations.art: A row of roofs of houses with a magnified view of tiny fibres, and a doctor's notebook showing a long-term study.
explanations.context: A material that does a job well today may cause trouble many years later. This card explains why engineers now look at the long term.

explanations.concept: Cost per use: why the cheapest is not always cheapest
explanations.definition: Cost per use is the price of a thing divided by the number of times, or years, you use it.
explanations.description: A steel tumbler costs 120 rupees. A plastic tumbler costs 20 rupees. At the shop, the plastic one is six times cheaper. But the steel one may last 20 years, and the plastic one may crack in 2. So the steel one costs 6 rupees a year, and the plastic one costs 10 rupees a year. For a cloth bag at 40 rupees and a plastic bag at 2 rupees, the cloth bag has paid for itself after 20 shopping trips. After that, every trip is free. This way of thinking is called cost per use or cost per year. It is not perfect. It does not count the cost of cleaning and mending, and it does not count the cost to the world. But it is a fairer way to compare than price alone. Many families already do this without noticing, when they buy a good pair of school shoes.
examples: A pair of 600 rupee shoes that lasts 2 years costs 300 rupees a year.
A pair of 300 rupee shoes that lasts 6 months costs 600 rupees a year.
A pressure cooker bought for 1,800 rupees and used for 10 years costs 180 rupees a year.
explanations.art: Two price tags, one with a big number beside a short row of tick marks and one with a small number beside a long row of tick marks.
explanations.context: A cheap thing that breaks can cost more in the end. This card explains cost per use, a fair way to compare what we buy.

explanations.concept: Reduce, reuse, repair, recycle: which comes first?
explanations.definition: Reduce means to make and buy less. Reuse means to use a thing again. Repair means to mend a thing. Recycle means to break it down and make something new.
explanations.description: People often say 'recycle'. But recycling uses energy and often makes weaker material, so it is the last of four steps. First is to reduce: do not make or buy the thing at all if you can do without it. Second is to reuse: use the thing again, perhaps for a new job. Third is to repair: mend it before it is thrown away. Last is to recycle: break it down and make something new from the material. A glass jar reused as a rice container uses no new energy at all. A shirt mended with a patch uses a bit of thread. Melting the same jar to make a new one takes a lot of heat. Metals such as steel and aluminium can be recycled many times with little loss. Paper loses strength each time. Mixed plastics are hard to sort and often cannot be made into good new things. The order tells us where the biggest saving is: not making in the first place.
examples: Reducing: carry a steel bottle so you never need a plastic one.
Reusing: a glass pickle jar becomes a jar for rice.
Repairing: a tailor mends a torn school bag.
explanations.art: A ladder of four steps with a child climbing: reduce at the bottom, then reuse, repair and recycle at the top, each step with a small picture.
explanations.context: People often say 'recycle', but it is the last choice, not the first. This card explains the order of four steps and why.

agreed.text: No material is best at everything. Every choice gives up something.
agreed.evidence: Every material tested by engineers has a weak side: steel rusts or is heavy, glass breaks, wood burns or rots, plastic lasts too long. Designers expect to trade one good thing for another.

agreed.text: The best material for a job depends on the place, the people and the price, as well as on the job.
agreed.evidence: Mud walls suit a dry desert village, steel and glass suit a city, and sloping tiled roofs suit rainy hills. The same job is done with different materials across India.

agreed.text: Two materials joined together can do what neither can do alone.
agreed.evidence: Mud with straw, concrete with steel bars, bone, wood and fibreglass are all composites. Their strength has been measured and is bigger than the strength of the parts.

agreed.text: Mixing a metal with other atoms usually makes it harder.
agreed.evidence: Bronze, brass and steel are all harder than the pure metals they are made from. Odd-sized atoms stop the layers of metal from sliding.

agreed.text: Every object has a whole life: its source, its making, its use and what happens after.
agreed.evidence: Engineers measure the energy and water used at each stage, and they measure what happens to a thing after it is thrown away. The amounts differ widely from one material to the next.

agreed.text: Some materials rot, some rust, some can be remade and some last a very long time, and this matters when we choose.
agreed.evidence: Bacteria and fungi break down plant and animal materials. Metals and glass can be melted again. Most plastics resist breaking down and stay in the ground for a very long time.

challenging.claim: Natural materials are always better than made ones.
challenging.who: Many people, and many adverts that say 'all natural'
challenging.for: Natural materials such as cotton, wood and clay come from sources that can grow back and usually rot at the end.
challenging.against: Natural does not always mean harmless or low-cost. Asbestos is a natural mineral that harms the lungs. Growing cotton can use a great deal of water. Some made materials, such as a steel pan that lasts forty years, can be kinder in the long run than something natural that is used once.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that anything natural is better than anything made.

challenging.claim: The strongest material is the best material.
challenging.who: A common idea, and the way many adverts talk
challenging.for: Strength is easy to measure, and a stronger material will not break as easily.
challenging.against: A super strong material may be too heavy, too costly, too hard to shape or too long-lasting. A school bag strap made of steel cable would be strong and useless. A good choice gives enough strength and then looks at everything else.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that the strongest material wins every time.

challenging.claim: Plastic is the problem, so we should stop using it everywhere.
challenging.for: Plastic waste fills landfills and rivers, breaks into microplastics and lasts for a very long time.
challenging.against: Plastic is also used to make helmets, syringes, water pipes and food packaging that keeps food from spoiling. The trouble is mostly the huge amount of plastic made to be used once and thrown away. Some scientists say we should use plastic where nothing else will do, and nowhere else.
challenging.context: This card is about whether plastic should be banned, or used with more care.

challenging.for: Recycling steel, aluminium and glass saves energy and raw material, and keeps them out of landfills.
challenging.against: Recycling takes energy, and often makes weaker material. Paper fibres get shorter each time. Many plastics are mixed and cannot be sorted well. Only a small part of the world's plastic has ever been recycled. Many scientists say the first steps are to make less and to reuse and mend what we have.
challenging.context: This card is about whether recycling is enough on its own.

challenging.claim: Old, traditional ways of choosing materials are just superstition.
challenging.who: Some people who prefer modern materials
challenging.for: Some old beliefs have not been tested, and a few are plainly wrong.
challenging.against: Many traditional choices, such as banana leaf plates, coir ropes, mud and lime walls and clay pots, have good reasons that can be tested. The iron pillar in Delhi has stood for about 1,500 years. A careful scientist tests old ideas, and neither throws them all away nor believes them all.
challenging.context: This card is about how much we should trust the choices of people who lived before laboratories.

challenging.claim: If something rots, it is automatically the greener choice.
challenging.for: Things that rot return to the soil and do not pile up.
challenging.against: A paper cup lined with plastic does not rot easily. Some 'compostable' plastics only break down in very hot industrial composters. A material that rots usually comes from plants, and growing and carrying the plants needs land, water and fuel. The honest answer comes from looking at the whole life, and often the best choice is something used many times.
challenging.context: This card is about whether 'biodegradable' always means better.

challenging.claim: The cheapest thing to buy is the cheapest thing to own.
challenging.who: Many shoppers, when money is short
challenging.for: When money is tight, a low price today is a real help.
challenging.against: A cheap thing that breaks soon may cost more per year than a dearer thing that lasts. Cost per use is a fairer way to compare. It is also unfair that poorer families often cannot afford the dearer thing that would save them money.
challenging.context: This card is about comparing what things cost over their whole lives.

big_questions.q: Paper alone bends, dried paste alone snaps, and the two together are strong. Where does the strength of the bar come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the paper does when the bar is pulled, and what the paste does.

big_questions.q: If there is no best material, what does it mean to choose well?
big_questions.hint: Think about how the winner in a decision matrix changes when we change what we care about.

big_questions.q: Whose job is it to decide what matters most when we choose a material: the maker, the buyer, the neighbour who will live near the factory, or the children who will live with the waste?
big_questions.hint: Think about who pays when a material's cost shows up later.

big_questions.q: A bamboo bridge, a steel bridge and a living root bridge can all cross a river. The living root bridge takes many years to grow, but it gets stronger every year. Is it cheaper or more expensive than the others?
big_questions.hint: Cost today and cost over fifty years can give different answers.

big_questions.q: Plastic lasts almost for ever. Is that a gift or a curse?
big_questions.hint: Think of a medicine bottle, and then of a bag used for ten minutes.

big_questions.q: A banana leaf, a steel spoon and a plastic bag are all made of atoms. Why do they have such different lives after we are done with them?
big_questions.hint: Think about how the atoms are joined, and who can break the joins apart.

big_questions.q: People long ago chose banana leaf plates for good reasons, without ever using a laboratory. How do we know if a tradition is wise?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you could test, and what you could not.

big_questions.q: Asbestos and lead did their jobs well, and turned out to harm people many years later. How can we choose well when we cannot see the future?
big_questions.hint: What could makers do before they use a new material everywhere?

big_questions.q: Everything we make comes from the ground, and goes back into the ground, the air or the sea. Is there such a thing as 'away' when we throw something away?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the atoms of a plastic bag are a hundred years from now.

big_questions.q: A girl in a village and a woman engineer in a city look at the same river. Why might they choose different bridges, and who should decide?
big_questions.hint: Think about place, price, who will use it and who will look after it.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, surgeons believed the body would fight any metal put inside it. They expected scar tissue to wall it off, or the body to push it out. Around 1952, in Lund in Sweden, a doctor named Per-Ingvar Brånemark was studying how bone heals. He screwed tiny titanium chambers into the leg bones of rabbits, so that he could watch the blood flow with a microscope. When the study was over, he tried to take the chambers out. They would not come out. The bone had grown tightly around the titanium and held it fast. Brånemark realised that bone could join itself to titanium without scar tissue. He called this joining osseointegration. Over the next years, with many tests, he and others made titanium roots for teeth, and later joints, which could last for years inside people. The old idea that metal in the body would always be rejected was wrong for titanium.
how_we_found_out.who: Per-Ingvar Brånemark, a Swedish doctor, and the colleagues who tested titanium after him
how_we_found_out.when: About 1952, with the first uses in people in the 1960s
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the body always walls off or pushes out metal placed inside it. In Brånemark's rabbit studies, bone grew so tightly onto titanium that the chambers could not be removed. This showed that the right material can join the body.
how_we_found_out.art: A doctor in a 1950s laboratory in Sweden holding a tiny titanium chamber beside a microscope, with a rabbit's leg bone drawn in cross-section showing bone grown tightly around the metal.

story.title: The Bridge That Is Never Finished
story.note: A made-up story. Living root bridges are real and are found in the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya. People guide the roots of the rubber fig tree, Ficus elastica, across rivers, sometimes along hollow trunks of betel-nut palms, and the roots thicken and join as they grow. Some bridges are many generations old, and the largest take many years to become usable. Daiaphi, her grandmother, the engineer and the village are imagined, and the names are only meant to sound like names from the hills. The steel rusting in the heavy rain is real.
text: Daiaphi lived in a village in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, one of the wettest parts of India. From June to September, the rain came down like a curtain, and the river below the village swelled until it roared. Every day, to reach her school on the far side, she crossed that river on a bridge made of roots.

The bridge was alive. It was made from the roots of a rubber fig tree that grew on the near bank. Long ago, the people of her village had led the roots across the river, along hollow trunks of betel-nut palm, and tied them in place. The roots had touched, and joined, and grown thick. Now the bridge was as wide as two people walking side by side, and it swayed a little, and it never broke.

Her grandmother, Kong Rimai, walked it every morning with a basket on her back. 'My grandmother helped to tie the first of these roots,' she said. 'I tied a few. You will tie some. This bridge is never finished.'

Daiaphi liked the idea. But one July, a flood came down the river and took away the planks of the old path that led to the bridge. A man arrived from the city of Shillong. His name was Mr. Das, and he was an engineer. He carried a roll of drawings under his arm.

'A steel bridge,' he told the village meeting. 'I can build it before next monsoon. Strong, quick, and no waiting. Steel is much stronger than roots.' Some of the men nodded. A bridge by next year sounded good.

Daiaphi was ten. She was sitting at the back. At school, her teacher had shown her a table with materials down the side and needs along the top. 'Excuse me,' she said, and everybody turned. 'What does the bridge need to do?'

They made the list on the ground with a stick. It must carry people and baskets. It must survive floods. It must last. It must not cost more than the village could pay. And it must not leave a mess when it was done. Mr. Das added one more: 'it must be ready soon'.

'So steel is strong,' said Daiaphi, drawing columns in the mud. 'Steel is quick. What happens to steel here?' She pointed to the iron railing by the school gate. It had been painted two years before. Orange rust had come through the paint in patches, and it flaked when she touched it.
Mr. Das went quiet. 'In heavy rain, steel needs paint every few years,' he admitted. 'And after thirty years or so, it must be replaced.'
'And where does the old steel go?' she asked. He rubbed his chin. 'To a scrap dealer in Shillong, if someone carries it that far. If not, to the river.'

Then Daiaphi took his hand and led him down to the root bridge. 'Hold this root,' she said. It was as thick as his leg. 'Pull.' He pulled. It did not move. 'This root was thinner than my arm when Kong's grandmother tied it. Every year it gets stronger. When a root is hurt in a flood, it grows back. And when the bridge is very old, it does not become rubbish. The tree is still alive.'

'But,' said Mr. Das, 'you wait twenty years for a new root bridge to be ready.' Kong Rimai had followed them. 'We wait for rice,' she said. 'We wait for children to grow. Waiting is not a cost, if you plan for it.'

Mr. Das opened his roll of drawings, and then he put it down. He took a pencil and a page. 'Teach me your table,' he said. So Daiaphi taught him. They put steel and roots along the side. They gave each need a weight. For 'ready soon', the weight was big. For 'lasts', and 'leaves no mess', the weight was big too. They gave scores. The totals were close.
'It depends,' said Mr. Das slowly. 'On what we count. If we count only next year, steel wins. If we count fifty years, the roots win.' 'Then count both,' said Daiaphi.

The village decided to do both. Mr. Das would build one small, light steel footbridge, quickly, for the village to cross while the old path was mended. And the next week, the village led new roots from the fig on the far bank, along fresh trunks of betel-nut palm, across the river. Daiaphi tied the first knot. It would not be ready for many years. By then she would be a grown woman, and her own children would cross.
story.epiphany: Steel wins if only next year counts. The roots win if fifty years count, and they leave no waste. Daiaphi sees this when she asks what the bridge must do, and scores both materials on every need. The best material depends on what we count. So the village uses both, and plans for the long run.
ask: What needs did the village list for the bridge?
Why did steel win when only next year counted, and the roots win when fifty years counted?
What happens to the old steel, and what happens to an old root bridge?
How did making a table help Mr. Das change his mind?
Why did the village decide to build both bridges?

games.title: Which Material, and What's the Catch?
games.context: This is a card game about choosing a material for a job. Each card names a job and three materials, and you choose one and name its catch.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a pile in the middle of a table, with a tray of tokens and a pencil and paper for the score.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile. Put the tokens in a bowl.

setup.art: A player reading a card aloud with three choices, and the others holding up fingers for 1, 2 or 3 for their choice.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Everyone holds up fingers to choose.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the good answers and the catch, with a token being passed to a player.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Win a token for a good choice, and one for naming the catch.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a job and three materials on the front, the good answers and the catches on the back

items.f: 1. A water bottle for a school bag in Chennai in May. Choose one: a steel flask, a glass bottle or a thin plastic bottle.
items.b: Good answers: steel flask or thin plastic. The steel flask keeps water cool, but it is heavy and costs more. The plastic bottle is light and cheap, but the water warms up. Glass is hard to carry safely, because it can break in a bag.

items.f: 2. A roof for a house in a hill village with very heavy monsoon rain. Choose one: clay tiles, a tin sheet or a thatch of grass.
items.b: All three can be good, each with a catch. Clay tiles shed water and keep the house cool, but they are heavy. A tin sheet is light, but loud and hot. Thatch is cheap and cool, but needs mending every few years.

items.f: 3. Plates for a wedding feast for 500 people. Choose one: steel plates, banana leaves or paper plates with a plastic lining.
items.b: Good answer: banana leaves. They are cheap, light, need no washing and rot afterwards. The catch is that leaves must be fresh. Steel plates must be washed 500 times. The lining on the paper plates does not rot.

items.f: 4. A wall for a house in the Thar desert, where the midday heat is fierce. Choose one: thick mud, thin tin or a thin glass window wall.
items.b: Good answer: thick mud. It heats slowly and keeps the inside cool in the day. The catch is that mud needs mending after rain. Thin tin and glass let the heat through quickly.

items.f: 5. A bag for the market. Choose one: a jute bag, a thin plastic bag or a paper bag.
items.b: Good answer: a jute bag. It carries a heavy load and can be used many times. The catch is that it costs more at first. A plastic bag is cheap and holds when wet, but it may last for a very long time in the ground. A paper bag is weak when wet.

items.f: 6. A spoon for stirring a hot pan. Choose one: a wooden spoon, a steel spoon or a plastic spoon.
items.b: Good answer: wooden. It does not get hot in the hand, and does not scratch the pan. The catch is that wood can crack or stain. A steel spoon gets hot. A plastic spoon can melt.

items.f: 7. The shell of a safety helmet. Choose one: hard plastic, wood or thick steel.
items.b: Good answer: hard plastic with a soft inner lining. It is light and absorbs a knock. A steel helmet is too heavy for daily use. Wood can split. The catch for plastic is that it can crack after a big knock and must be replaced.

items.f: 8. A small bridge over a stream in a village. Choose one: bamboo, steel or a living root bridge.
items.b: All three can be good. Bamboo is quick, cheap and renewable, but it rots in a few years. Steel is strong and quick, but needs paint. Living roots take many years to grow, but last for generations and mend themselves.

items.f: 9. A cricket bat. Choose one: willow wood, solid steel or thick foam.
items.b: Good answer: willow wood. It is light and springy, and the ball bounces off it well. The catch is that wood can crack and needs oiling. Steel would be too heavy and would dent. Foam would not drive a ball far.

items.f: 10. A water pipe inside a house. Choose one: PVC plastic, steel or clay.
items.b: Good answers: PVC plastic or steel. PVC is light, cheap and does not rust, but may crack in strong sun. Steel is tough but rusts. Clay pipes crack easily when pushed or knocked.

items.f: 11. A classroom window. Choose one: glass, clear plastic sheet or cloth.
items.b: Good answer: glass. It is clear and hard to scratch. The catch is that it breaks. Clear plastic sheets are safer but scratch and go yellow in sunlight. Cloth keeps out light and does not keep out rain.

items.f: 12. A water store for a summer in a village home. Choose one: a clay matka, a steel drum or a plastic tank.
items.b: Good answer: a clay matka for drinking water, because a little water seeps through the clay and keeps the rest cool. The catch is that it is heavy and can crack. A steel drum lasts long, but the water in it gets warm. A plastic tank is light, but the water in it gets warm too.

items.f: 13. A raincoat. Choose one: cotton, plastic-coated cloth or paper.
items.b: Good answer: plastic-coated cloth. It keeps water out, and is light. The catch is that it does not let sweat out, and it lasts a very long time as waste. Cotton soaks up water. Paper falls apart.

items.f: 14. A tooth root or a joint inside a human body. Choose one: titanium, wood or ordinary iron.
items.b: Good answer: titanium. Bone grows tightly onto titanium, and it does not rust in body fluids. The catch is that it is costly. Wood would rot. Iron would rust.

items.f: 15. Packing for a box of eggs on a bus. Choose one: crumpled paper, plastic foam or a steel box.
items.b: Good answers: crumpled paper or foam. Both soak up a bump. Crumpled paper rots and is cheap. Foam is light but lasts a very long time as waste. A steel box would be too heavy and would not cushion.

items.f: 16. A floor for a kitchen in Kerala in the wet season. Choose one: polished marble, rough stone tiles or wood.
items.b: Good answer: rough stone tiles. They do not soak up water, and grip when wet. Polished marble becomes slippery when wet. Wood can swell and rot in the damp.

items.f: 17. A fishing net. Choose one: coir, nylon or silk thread.
items.b: Good answers: nylon for strength, or coir for harbour work. Nylon is strong and light, but lost nets last a very long time in the sea. Coir rots away if lost. Silk is too costly and weak when wet.

items.f: 18. A chair for a school in Leh in winter. Choose one: all-steel, wood or hard plastic.
items.b: Good answer: wood. It is not icy to sit on. The catch is that wood can warp. A steel chair feels very cold, because metal draws heat from your body. Hard plastic can crack in the cold.

items.f: 19. A snack packet that must keep crisps fresh for months. Choose one: thin plastic film, plain paper or a glass jar.
items.b: Good answer: thin plastic film, often with a layer of metal foil. It keeps out air and damp and is light to carry. The catch is that it is almost impossible to recycle. Glass jars are heavy to carry. Paper lets in damp.

items.f: 20. A drinking cup for a tea stall. Choose one: a clay kullad, a paper cup or a steel tumbler.
items.b: All three can be good. A clay kullad is cheap, needs no washing and crumbles back to clay, but it is heavy and breaks. A paper cup is light but is often lined with plastic. A steel tumbler lasts for years but must be washed.

rules: Cut out the 20 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down.
The reader turns over the top card and reads the front aloud, including the job and all three materials.
Each player chooses one material. Everyone shows their choice at the same time by holding up one, two or three fingers, for the first, second or third material on the card.
Each player says the catch of the material they chose. The catch is what it is bad at.
Turn the card over and read the back. A player who chose a good answer wins one token.
A player who named a catch that is on the back, or a good true catch of their own, wins one more token.
If the group agrees that a player's own reason is good, the parent can give a token, even if it is not on the back.
After all the cards, the player with most tokens wins. If it is a tie, the winners share.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Shuffle them and put them face down. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl. 4. Choose a first reader.
flow.say: Every card has a job and three materials. No material is perfect. We each choose one material and say its catch, which is what it is bad at.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Put out the tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Material, and What's the Catch?, a game about choosing materials for jobs.
flow.parent: Works with one child and a parent, or 2 to 4 children. The reader changes after each card. The youngest player can read the first card with help.

flow.do: Play the first card as practice. After choosing, ask the question below, and do not turn the card over yet.
flow.say: Choose a material for this job. What is the catch of your choice?
flow.kid: Choose. Say the catch.

ask.q: What does your chosen material do badly?
good: It lasts too long as waste.

flow.parent: If a child cannot name a catch, ask: would this material still be a good choice in a different place, or for a different person?
flow.context: In this step, you practise with one card, to learn how to name a catch.

flow.do: Play cards 2 to 16. After every five cards, ask the question below.
flow.say: Read the card. Choose. Name the catch. Check the back.
flow.kid: Read, choose, name the catch, check.

ask.q: Did any card have only one right answer?
good: Often the best choice depended on the place.

check.q: A material is strong, cheap and quick to make, but it lasts a very long time in the ground. Which statement is fair?
options: It is a trade-off. It can be a good choice for some jobs and a poor choice for others
It is the worst material
It is the best material
check.why: Whether a material is good or bad depends on the job and the place. A long-lasting material is a gain for a bridge and a problem for a bag used for ten minutes. Choosing 'worst' or 'best' usually means looking at only one side.

flow.context: In this step, you play most of the cards. Notice that more than one material can be a good choice.

flow.do: Play the last four cards. Count the tokens and name the winner.
flow.say: Last cards. Then count the tokens.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count the tokens.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards and count the score.

flow.do: Ask each player to think of one job at home and choose a material for it. What would they choose, and what is the catch?
flow.say: Think of a job at home. Which material would you choose? What is its catch?
flow.kid: Pick a job at home. Name a material and its catch.
flow.context: This is the last step of the game. You use what you learned on a real job at home.

games.title: Where Does It Go?
games.context: This is a sorting game about what happens to a thing after we are done with it. You put each object on the mat where you think it will end up.

setup.art: Four mats on a floor labelled Rots, Rusts, Remade and Stays a very long time, with a pile of cards in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Put out the four mats and the pile of cards.

setup.art: A child holding a card of a banana leaf plate and placing it on the Rots mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put it on the mat where it will end up.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the right mat and a reason.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: an object on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: 1. A banana leaf plate.
items.b: Rots. It breaks down in a few weeks in damp soil.

items.f: 2. A steel katori.
items.b: Remade. Steel can be melted and made into new things again and again. A katori can also be used for decades.

items.f: 3. A glass bottle.
items.b: Remade. Glass can be melted and made into new bottles with little loss. It can also be washed and refilled.

items.f: 4. A sheet of newspaper.
items.b: It can rot or be remade. In damp soil it rots in weeks to months. It can also be pulped and made into paper a few times, getting weaker each time.

items.f: 5. A thin plastic carry bag.
items.b: Stays a very long time. It breaks into tiny pieces but does not rot. In some places it can be recycled.

items.f: 6. A cotton shirt.
items.b: Rots, but slowly. In warm damp soil it can take months to years. Old cotton can also be shredded and made into new paper or cloth.

items.f: 7. A polyester shirt.
items.b: Stays a very long time. It is a plastic, and it also sheds tiny threads called microplastics each time it is washed.

items.f: 8. A sheet of kitchen aluminium foil.
items.b: Remade. Aluminium can be melted and made into new things again and again. Clean foil is easier to recycle.

items.f: 9. A coconut shell.
items.b: Rots, slowly. It is hard, so it can take many months to years. It can also be reused as a ladle or a bowl, or burned as fuel.

items.f: 10. A plastic water bottle made of PET.
items.b: It can be remade, or it stays. In many places PET bottles are melted and made into new things. If nobody collects the bottle, experts say it stays for hundreds of years. Nobody has watched one for long enough to see it break down fully.

items.f: 11. A clay kullad.
items.b: Stays, but harmlessly. Fired clay does not rot, and it breaks into clay pieces that join the soil. Archaeologists still dig up clay pieces from thousands of years ago.

items.f: 12. A banana peel.
items.b: Rots. It breaks down in days to weeks, and feeds the soil.

items.f: 13. An iron nail.
items.b: Rusts. In damp air it slowly turns to rust. It can also be collected as scrap and melted.

items.f: 14. A woollen sweater.
items.b: Rots, slowly. Wool is made by sheep, so living things can break it down. It can take months to years.

items.f: 15. A foam cup.
items.b: Stays a very long time. It is a plastic foam, and it breaks into tiny pieces but does not rot.

items.f: 16. A wooden spoon.
items.b: Rots, slowly. It can take years in damp soil. A wooden spoon can also be reused for years in the kitchen.

items.f: 17. A tin food can made of steel.
items.b: Rusts and is remade. A steel can will rust in damp soil, and it can also be collected and melted into new steel.

items.f: 18. A paper cup with a plastic lining.
items.b: Tricky. The paper rots, but the thin plastic lining stays. It is hard to recycle because the two layers are stuck together.

items.f: 19. A leather chappal.
items.b: Rots, slowly. Leather is made from animal skin. It can take years, and any rubber or plastic sole will stay.

items.f: 20. A bar of steel from an old bridge.
items.b: Remade. Steel from old bridges is melted and made into new steel.

printables.title: Four mats
items: ROTS: living things such as bacteria and fungi break the thing down into soil
RUSTS: iron slowly turns to crumbly rust
REMADE: it can be melted or pulped and made into new things

Take the top card and read the front aloud. Do not look at the back.
Put the card on the mat where you think the thing will end up.
Turn the card over and read the answer. If you were right, take one token.

If you play with others, take turns. The player with most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the four mats. 2. Shuffle the 20 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Today we sort things by what happens to them after we finish with them. There are four mats: rots, rusts, remade and stays.
flow.kid: Put out the four mats. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does It Go?, a sorting game about the end of a thing's life.

flow.do: Read the four mats aloud. Ask the question below before the first card.
flow.say: What does rots mean? What does rusts mean? What does remade mean? What does stays mean?
flow.kid: Read the four mats. Say what each one means.

ask.q: What is the difference between rots and rusts?
good: Rotting is living things breaking something down.
Rusting is iron slowly turning orange with air and water.

flow.context: In this step, you check what each mat means before you start.

flow.do: Play cards 1 to 14. Turn each card over after you place it. Read the reason aloud.
flow.say: Read a card. Put it on a mat. Then check the back.
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a mat. Check the back.

check.q: A clay kullad is broken. Which mat fits best?
options: Stays a very long time, but harmlessly, as clay pieces
Rots, because clay is natural
Rusts, because clay is a metal
check.why: Fired clay does not rot or rust. It breaks into smaller clay pieces that join the soil. 'Stays' does not always mean harmful. Picking 'rots' usually comes from thinking that anything natural rots.

flow.context: In this step, you play most of the game and learn what happens to common things.

flow.do: Play the last six cards. Count the tokens.
flow.say: The last cards. Then count the tokens.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count the tokens.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards.

flow.do: Ask each player to pick one thing they used today and say which mat it will end up on. Ask: could it be on a different mat?
flow.say: Think of one thing you used today. Where will it end up? Could it end up somewhere else?
flow.kid: Pick a thing you used today. Where will it end up?
flow.context: This is the last step of the game. You look at your own day.

experiments.title: Paper and Paste: is a layered bar stronger than its parts?

schedule.what: Guess. Make the paste and the four kinds of bar, two of each. Set them to dry.
Test all eight bars across a gap with a hanging cup of water. Draw the chart and write what you found.

experiments.question: A strip of paper bends easily. A dried bar of flour paste snaps easily. Is a bar of paper layers glued with paste stronger than either one alone? And is paste with tiny fibres mixed in stronger than plain paste?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which of the four bars will hold the most water in a hanging cup before it snaps or sags? Which will hold the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All four kinds of bar are the same length and width. They use the same newspaper and the same paste. They dry in the same place for the same time. They rest across the same gap, and water is poured in at the same slow speed. The order in which the bars are tested is picked by drawing chits from a bowl. Only what the bar is made of changes. Two bars of each kind show how much each kind varies.
results_table: How it failed: snapped or sagged

materials.item: 4 sheets of old newspaper
6 level tablespoons of maida or plain wheat flour, a pinch of salt and about 8 tablespoons of cold water, in a bowl
a plastic carry bag, cut open flat, to dry the bars on
a few tissue paper shreds or cotton wool fibres, about one tablespoon
scissors used by a grown-up, a ruler, a pencil and masking tape
a tray or board to dry the bars on
2 piles of books of equal height, with a gap of 12 centimetres between them
a small paper or plastic cup (about 200 ml) and thread, to hang under the bar. For a bar that holds more than the cup, use a mug with a handle
a jug of water and a medicine cup or a measuring cup marked in millilitres. If you have neither, count tablespoons (one level tablespoon is about 15 ml)
8 paper chits and a bowl to draw the order

experiments.safety: The paste is flour and water, but do not eat it or the bars. If a bar grows mould while drying, do not sniff it. Throw it away and make another. Only a grown-up should use the scissors. Wash your hands after touching the paste. Keep a tray under the cup so the water does not wet the floor. Maida is wheat flour, so a child with a wheat allergy should not handle the dry flour or the paste.
experiments.record: Write what each bar was made of. Write the water each bar held in millilitres and how it failed. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each kind, using the bigger of the two results. Work out how many times stronger the layered bar was than the paste bar and than the paper stack.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make four kinds of bar from newspaper and flour paste, dry them for two days, and test how much water each can hold. You find out whether two weak things together can be strong.

setup.art: A bowl of white flour paste being stirred with a spoon, beside a stack of newspaper strips cut 4 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long.
setup.caption: 1. Stir the paste. Cut newspaper strips 4 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long.

setup.art: Four bars labelled A, B, C and D lying on a plastic sheet: A is plain paste, B is a stack of dry paper, C is four layers of paper glued with paste, and D is paste with tissue shreds.
setup.caption: 2. Make the four bars and label them A, B, C and D.

setup.art: A bar resting across a gap between two piles of books, with a small cup hanging by a thread from its middle and a ruler standing beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Rest a bar across the gap and hang a cup from its middle.

setup.art: A hand pouring water slowly from a jug into the cup while the bar bends, and a ruler showing the sag.
setup.caption: 4. Pour water slowly until the bar snaps or sinks 2 centimetres.

setup.art: A bar chart drawn on paper with four bars, one for each kind of bar.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a bar chart of the results.

flow.do: Show your child the paper, the paste and the tissue shreds. Ask which bar they think will hold the most water and which the least, and why.
flow.say: We will make four kinds of bar. One is paste. One is a stack of paper. One is paper glued with paste. One is paste with fibres. Which holds the most? Which holds the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four bars. Which holds the most water? Which holds the least? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that bar will hold the most?
good: Paper is strong and paste glues it.

ask.q: Which bar will be the weakest? Why?
good: The paste alone, because it is brittle.
The loose paper, because it bends.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Write each guess with the reason. After the test, come back to these guesses.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper and Paste. You guess before you build.

flow.do: 1. Mix 6 level tablespoons of flour with a pinch of salt in a bowl. 2. Add cold water a spoon at a time, until the paste is smooth and thick like curd. 3. Cut 16 newspaper strips (4 for each of bars B and C, two bars of each), each 4 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long.
flow.say: Make the paste smooth, with no lumps. It should be as thick as curd. The pinch of salt may help slow the mould.
flow.kid: Mix flour and water into a paste. Cut the paper into strips.
flow.parent: Use the paste cold. There is no need to cook it. One batch makes all eight bars for one child. With 2 or more children, each child makes their own batch and one bar of each kind (A, B, C and D). Two children's bars together give the two bars of each kind. Each bar is tested by a different child from the one who made it. Cut all the strips the same size with a ruler. Strips cut with the grain, along the long side of the newspaper, are stronger. What matters most is that all the strips are cut in the same direction.
flow.context: In this step, you make the paste and cut the paper.

flow.do: Bar A: spread a layer of paste about 3 millimetres thick, 20 centimetres by 4 centimetres, on a plastic sheet. Bar B: stack 4 dry strips of paper, and lay them next to the others. Bar C: brush paste on 4 strips, stack them and press flat. Bar D: stir a tablespoon of tissue shreds into some paste, and spread it like bar A. Make two bars of each kind.
flow.say: Bar A is plain paste. Bar B is four dry strips. Bar C is four strips glued with paste. Bar D is paste with shreds. Two of each.
flow.kid: Make two of each bar. Label them A, B, C and D.
flow.parent: Bar B is not glued. It is just a stack of paper, for comparison. Keep paste thickness the same in A and D. Press C flat with your palm and smooth out bubbles. Make the paste layers about 2 to 3 millimetres thick. A thicker layer cracks and curls as it dries. Label each bar with tape and a letter on the plastic sheet.

check.q: Why do we make two bars of each kind?
options: To see how much one kind varies, and not trust a single bar
Because one bar will break first
To use up the paper
check.why: One bar may have a hidden flaw. Two bars of the same kind show how much that kind varies. Then you can tell whether the difference between two kinds is bigger than that. Picking 'one will break' misses the point.

flow.context: In this step, you build the bars. Each kind is made twice, so you can see how much one kind varies.

flow.do: Put the bars on a tray in a warm, shady place, such as a shelf near a window. Do not touch them. Write down the date and the time. They need two days to dry.
flow.say: The bars need two full days to dry. Do not touch them. Keep them out of the rain.
flow.kid: Put the bars on a tray. Leave them for two days.
flow.parent: If the weather is very damp, dry the bars near a fan, or give them three or four days. Flour paste 3 millimetres thick can take longer than two days in monsoon damp. Press a bar with a fingernail: it is ready when it is hard all through. Bars may curl a little at the edges. Press them flat under a book for the last hour. If a bar grows white or green mould, throw the bar away and make another. A bar that is still soft in the middle will be weak, so wait until it feels hard and dry all through.
flow.context: In this step, you set the bars to dry. The test is two days later.

flow.do: Day 3. 1. Stand the two piles of books 12 centimetres apart. 2. Peel the dry bars off the plastic. 3. Make a small loop of thread to hang the cup from. 4. Stand a ruler beside the gap, to measure how far the middle of a bar sinks.
flow.say: Today we test. The bar rests across the gap. A cup hangs from its middle. We pour water into the cup slowly.
flow.kid: Set up the gap and the cup. Peel the bars off the plastic.

ask.q: Why do we pick the order of testing by drawing chits from a bowl?
good: So no bar always goes first.
So the tester cannot favour a bar.

flow.parent: If bar A or D breaks when you peel it off, write 'broke before testing' and use the spare bar. If both break, record 0 and keep the pieces to look at.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the test rig. Take care when you peel bar A, which may be brittle.

flow.do: Draw a chit from the bowl to pick the first bar. Rest that bar across the gap. Hang the empty cup from its middle. Pour water into the cup from the jug, slowly and steadily. Stop when the bar snaps or the middle sinks 2 centimetres. Pour the water from the cup into a medicine cup and read the millilitres. Test all eight bars in this way.
flow.say: Rest the bar across the gap. Hang the cup. Pour slowly. Stop when the bar snaps or sinks two centimetres. Measure the water.
flow.kid: Test one bar at a time. Pour slowly. Measure the water.
flow.parent: The cup itself weighs a little, so the same cup is used each time. Pour at the same speed. Keep a tray under the cup. Bar B, the loose paper stack, usually sags with only a few millilitres, and that is a good result. Bar C may hold more than a cup of water. If the cup is full and the bar has not failed, empty the cup into the measuring cup, write it down, refill and carry on, then add the totals. Roles for 2 to 4 children: one pours, one watches the ruler and says stop, one reads the millilitres, one writes. Swap roles for each bar.
flow.context: In this step, you test each bar. One millilitre of water weighs about one gram.

flow.do: Write the results in the table. Draw a bar chart. Work out how many times more water the layered bar C held than bar A, and than bar B. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Draw the chart. How many times more did bar C hold than bar A? Than bar B? Write your claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.kid: Draw the chart. Compare bar C with A and B.

ask.q: Is bar C stronger than its parts? Why do you think so?
good: Yes, because the paper carries the pull and the paste holds the layers.
Yes, because the layers cannot slide.

ask.q: What happened to bar D, the paste with fibres?
good: It held more than the plain paste.

flow.parent: A good reasoning sentence: the paste alone is brittle and the paper alone bends, but the paste holds the paper layers together so they cannot slide, and the paper stops cracks running through the paste. If bar B held 0 ml, write "less than 1 ml" and say bar C held "many times more", not an exact number. If bar D did better than bar A, the fibres stopped cracks. If not, say so honestly.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the numbers into a chart and write what you found.

flow.do: Look closely at a broken end of bar C. Look for paper fibres sticking out. Talk about what you see.
flow.say: Look at the broken end of bar C. What sticks out? What do you think the fibres were doing?
flow.kid: Look at the broken end of bar C. What sticks out?

check.q: What is the matrix in bar C?
options: The flour paste that holds the paper layers
The newspaper
The water in the cup
check.why: In a composite, the matrix holds the fibres and shares the load. In bar C, the paste is the matrix and the paper is the fibre. Choosing 'the newspaper' mixes up the fibre and the matrix.

flow.context: In this step, you look at how the bar failed.

experiments.title: The Burial Test: what does soil do to our scraps?

schedule.what: Guess. Bury six scraps in damp soil, and a seventh cup with soil only.
Look through the side of each cup. Do not dig.
Dig out each scrap, score it, tear it and compare it with its spare. Sort the scraps and write what you found.

experiments.question: After two weeks in damp soil, which of six scraps will have rotted, which will have changed a little and which will look the same as the day you buried them?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which scraps will rot, which will change a little and which will stay the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each scrap is the same size and goes in the same kind of soil, in the same kind of cup, in the same place. Each cup gets the same amount of water on the same days. One cup holds soil with nothing in it, as a control. A spare piece of each scrap is kept dry in an envelope to compare at the end. Only the scrap changes.
results_table: What it looked like on day 7 (through the cup)
Score on day 14, from 0 for unchanged to 4 for gone
How easily it tore on day 14, compared with the spare piece

materials.item: 7 clear plastic or glass cups or jars, all the same size (clear disposable cups from a kirana or curd tubs will do)
soil from a flowerpot or a garden, enough to fill the 7 cups, and a spoon
a piece of cotton cloth, a piece of polyester cloth, a piece of newspaper, a piece of plastic carry bag, a piece of kitchen foil and a banana peel, each about 5 centimetres square
a spare 5 centimetre piece of each of the cloths, the paper, the bag and the foil, kept in an envelope
a marker and sticky tape for labels, and a notebook
washing-up gloves and a plate
a spoon of water for each cup every three days

experiments.safety: Wash your hands after touching soil, and do not put your fingers in your mouth. Do not sniff the cups, because mould spores are not good to breathe in. Use gloves when you dig out the scraps. A grown-up should dig if the child has asthma or a mould allergy. Banana peel can attract fruit flies, so keep the cups loosely covered. A grown-up should cut the foil and plastic with scissors. Keep the cups away from babies and pets. Throw the soil and scraps away outside when you finish.
experiments.record: Write down what you see through the side of each cup on day 7. On day 14, give each scrap a score from 0 to 4. Tear each dug-up piece and its spare, and write which is easier to tear. Draw a table, and then sort the scraps into rots, changed a little and unchanged.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you bury six scraps in damp soil for two weeks and see what comes back to the earth. You score each scrap, and you keep a spare dry piece to compare.

setup.art: Seven clear cups in a row on a bright shelf, each with damp soil and a different scrap pressed against the glass at the side.
setup.caption: 1. Bury a scrap in each cup, near the glass. Leave one cup with soil only.
