setup.art: A child sprinkling a spoonful of water on a cup and a label with the scrap's name and the date.
setup.caption: 2. Label each cup and sprinkle a spoonful of water every three days.

setup.art: A child looking at a cup from the side and drawing what is visible in a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Look through the side of the cup on day 7.

setup.art: A child wearing gloves lifting a scrap from the soil with a spoon, and a spare dry piece in an envelope beside it.
setup.caption: 4. On day 14, lift out each scrap and compare it with its spare.

flow.do: Show your child the six scraps. For each scrap, ask whether it will rot, change a little or stay the same, and why.
flow.say: Here are six scraps. We will bury them in damp soil. Which will rot? Which will stay the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Six scraps. Which will rot? Which will stay the same? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that scrap will rot?
Why do you think that scrap will stay the same?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Write each guess in the table. Some children think that anything from a plant rots at the same speed. The test will show whether that is true.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Burial Test. You guess before you bury.

flow.do: 1. Cut each scrap to about 5 centimetres square. 2. Cut a spare piece of each and put the spares in an envelope. 3. Fill each cup three-quarters full with soil. 4. Dampen the soil with a spoon of water. 5. Press a scrap against the glass of each cup and cover it with soil.
flow.say: Fill each cup with soil. Dampen the soil. Press one scrap against the glass. Cover it. Label the cup.
flow.kid: Fill the cups. Press a scrap against the glass. Cover it.
flow.parent: Seven cups: one for each of six scraps, and one with soil only. Put the cups in a warm, shady place such as a balcony or a windowsill, but not in direct hot sun. Loosely cover the tops with a plate or paper, so that flies stay out and air gets in. With 2 to 4 children, everyone makes a guess for all six scraps, but each child buries and looks after only two cups. One child looks after the soil-only cup. On day 14 each child reports to the others.

check.q: Why do we keep a cup with soil only and no scrap?
options: As a control, to see what the soil does by itself
So there are seven cups
To save soil
check.why: A control gets everything except the thing being tested. The soil-only cup shows what changes in the soil itself, such as mould or damp. Picking 'seven cups' misses the purpose.

flow.context: In this step, you bury the scraps. Press each one against the side of the cup so you can watch it.

flow.do: Every three days, touch the soil. It should feel like a squeezed-out sponge. If it feels dry, sprinkle one or two spoons of water on the cup. If it feels wet or sticky, add no water and leave the cover off for a day. In hot dry weather you may need water more often. In the monsoon, you need less. Write the date on the label.
flow.say: Every three days, touch the soil. If it feels dry, add a spoon or two of water. Keep the soil damp, not wet.
flow.kid: Check the soil every three days. Add a little water if it is dry.
flow.context: In this step, you keep the soil damp. Damp soil is where bacteria and fungi do their work.

flow.do: Day 7. Look at each cup from the side. Do not dig. Draw or describe each scrap. Which has changed?
flow.say: Day seven. Look from the side. Do not dig. What has changed? What has stayed the same?
flow.kid: Look from the side. Do not dig. What has changed?

ask.q: Which scrap has changed the most so far?
Which have not changed at all?

flow.parent: By day 7, the banana peel is usually brown and soft, and may have white or grey mould. The paper may be darker and soft. The rest usually look the same. If you see mould, that is normal. Do not open the cups and do not sniff them. Different scraps may change first in your home, because the weather changes how fast things rot.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the scraps halfway. Do not touch them yet.

flow.do: Day 14. Put on gloves. Lift out each scrap with a spoon and put it on a plate. Score it from 0 to 4. Tear it, and tear its spare, and compare. Write everything down. Then put it all in the outdoor bin.
flow.say: Day fourteen. Put on gloves. Lift out each scrap. Score it. Tear it. Tear its spare piece too. Which tears more easily?
flow.kid: Wear gloves. Lift out each scrap. Score it. Tear it.
flow.parent: Score 0 is unchanged. Score 1 is stained or slightly soft. Score 2 is soft with holes. Score 3 is mostly gone. Score 4 is gone. Cotton often scores only 1 or 2 after two weeks. That is a real result. Cotton can take months to rot fully. Be honest about what you see.

check.q: The polyester cloth looks the same after two weeks. Does that mean it will never rot?
options: No. It means it did not change in two weeks, and tells us it changes very slowly or not at all
Yes, it never rots
It means the test was done wrongly
check.why: Two weeks is a short time. A test shows what happened in that time, not what happens for ever. The polyester is a plastic and very likely lasts for a very long time, but this test cannot prove it. Choosing 'never' goes further than the evidence.

flow.context: In this step, you dig out the scraps and compare them with the spares.

flow.do: Look at the results table. Sort the scraps into rots, changed a little and unchanged. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning, and one thing that your test could not tell you.
flow.say: Sort the scraps into three groups. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning. What did the test not tell you?
flow.kid: Sort the scraps. Write claim, evidence and reasoning.

ask.q: What do the scraps that rotted have in common?
What do the scraps that stayed the same have in common?

flow.parent: A good claim: the banana peel and the newspaper rotted fastest because they come from plants, and bacteria and fungi can break down plant material. The foil and the plastic did not change in two weeks. Remind your child that cotton also comes from a plant, but is slower.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the scraps and say what you can honestly claim.

activities.title: Score the Cup: a decision matrix for a drinking cup

materials.item: 4 different cups from the kitchen: a steel tumbler, a plastic cup, a paper cup and a glass or clay cup (a clay kullad costs a few rupees at a tea stall)
a jug of hot water, as hot as tea that you can sip, from a flask or a kettle that has rested for a few minutes, poured by a grown-up. Keep a little cold water in a second jug
a paper napkin and a plate
paper and a pencil to draw the table
a calculator, if you like

schedule.what: Test each cup for weight, comfort in the hand and leaking. Ask the price and how long it lasts. Score the cups for two different jobs. Add up and compare.

activities.record: A table with a row for each cup and a column for each need: light, comfortable to hold with warm water, does not leak, cost per year and what happens after. Scores from 1 to 5, a weight for each need, and a total for each cup, for two different jobs.
activities.context: In this activity, you test four cups, score them in a decision matrix for two different jobs, and see how the winner changes with the job.

setup.art: Four cups in a row on a table, a steel tumbler, a plastic cup, a paper cup and a glass cup, each on a paper napkin.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the four cups on paper napkins.

setup.art: A child holding the outside of each cup after hot drinking water has been poured into it by a grown-up.
setup.caption: 2. Pour hot drinking-temperature water into each cup and hold the outside for 20 seconds.

setup.art: A table on paper with the four cups down the side and five needs across the top, with weights and totals.
setup.caption: 3. Score each cup and add up the totals.

flow.do: Show your child the four cups. Ask which they think is the best cup, and why. Write it down. Then say that cups have different jobs. One job is a cup for a school bag. Another is a cup for a hot day at a tea stall.
flow.say: Here are four cups. Which is the best cup? Why do you think so? Does the best cup change with the job?
flow.kid: Four cups. Which is best? Does it depend on the job?

ask.q: Is there a best cup for every job?
good: No, it depends on the job.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. Some children will say steel because it does not break. Come back to this at the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of Score the Cup. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Lift each cup and score its weight from 1 to 5. A light cup scores 5. 2. A grown-up pours about 100 millilitres of hot water into each cup, one at a time. The water must be cool enough to sip. 3. Touch the outside of the cup. If it is comfortable, hold it for 20 seconds. Let go if it feels too hot. Score how comfortable it is from 1 to 5. 4. Pour the water out. Fill each cup with cold water and leave it on a napkin for 10 minutes. Score leaks from 1 to 5.
flow.say: Lift each cup and score its weight. Then a grown-up pours in warm water. Hold the outside of the cup and score how comfortable it is. Then fill each cup with cold water, leave it on a napkin for ten minutes, and score leaks.
flow.kid: Lift each cup. Hold the warm cup. Check the leaks.
flow.parent: Use water you could sip, never boiling water. Tap water that is only warm feels the same in every cup, so use hot water from a flask. The steel cup and the glass cup will usually feel hottest. A coated paper cup often does not leak at all, while an unglazed clay cup may sweat on the outside. If nothing leaks, give all cups a 5. That is a real result. Handle the glass cup with care. With 2 to 4 children, each child scores alone first, then compare. If scores differ, discuss why. Roles: one pours (a grown-up), one times, one writes. Write the scores down as you go.
flow.context: In this step, you test the cups for weight, comfort and leaks. A leak shows up as a wet patch on the napkin.

flow.do: Ask a grown-up what each cup cost and how long it lasts in years. Divide the price by the years to get the cost for each year. Score the lowest cost 5 and the highest cost 1. Then ask what happens to each cup after use. Score the cups that rot or can be remade higher.
flow.say: Ask the price and how many years each cup lasts. Divide the price by the years. The cup that costs least for each year scores 5.
flow.kid: Ask the price and the years. Divide price by years.

check.q: A steel tumbler costs 120 rupees and lasts 20 years. A paper cup costs 2 rupees and lasts one use. Which costs less for each use?
options: It depends on how many times you use the tumbler. After 60 uses the tumbler costs less for each use
The paper cup, because it is cheaper to buy
The steel tumbler, because it is stronger
check.why: 120 rupees divided by 60 uses is 2 rupees, the same as the paper cup. After more than 60 uses, the tumbler is cheaper for each use. Choosing 'the paper cup' looks only at the price today.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the cost for each year and what happens after.

flow.do: Make the matrix. Job 1 is a cup for a school bag. Give weights: light 3, does not leak 3, cost 2, comfort 1 and what happens after 1. Multiply each score by its weight. Add up the totals for each cup.
flow.say: Job one is a school bag cup. Give each need a weight. Multiply each score by its weight. Add up each row.
flow.kid: Make the matrix for a school bag cup. Add up the totals.
flow.parent: Walk through one row together before they do the rest. Check the multiplication. If two cups tie, discuss which need would break the tie.
flow.context: In this step, you build the decision matrix for the first job.

flow.do: Job 2 is a cup for a hot day at a tea stall, used 200 times a day. Change the weights: cost has weight 3, comfort has weight 3, what happens after has weight 2, light has weight 1. Work out the new totals. Did the best cup change?
flow.say: Job two is a tea stall. Change the weights. Work out the new totals. Did the winner change?
flow.kid: Change the weights for the tea stall. Did the winner change?

ask.q: Did the winner change? What made it change?
good: No, the same cup won both times.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child does one job's matrix, then they swap and check each other's sums. A good point to discuss: the scores are your judgement, not facts. Two families could disagree. Ask: what would make you change a score?
flow.context: In this step, you score the same cups for a second job. The winner may change.

activities.title: Follow a Thing: from the ground to the bin

materials.item: one object from home: a steel katori, a plastic bottle, a cotton shirt or a pencil
paper and coloured pencils to draw the four stages
a grown-up to ask questions

schedule.what: Choose an object. Draw its source, making, use and after. Ask what you do not know.

activities.record: A drawing of a circle with four stages: source, making, use and after, with notes under each, and a list of three questions that you cannot yet answer.
activities.context: In this activity, you follow one object through its whole life, from the ground it came from to the place it ends up, and you write down what you do not yet know.

setup.art: A katori on a table beside a drawing of a circle with four boxes: ground, factory, kitchen and scrapyard.
setup.caption: 1. Choose an object and draw four boxes in a circle.

setup.art: A child writing notes under each box, with a grown-up answering questions.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in each box with what you know and what you can find out.

setup.art: A list of three questions with question marks, beside the finished circle.
setup.caption: 3. Write three questions that you cannot yet answer.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose one object and say what it is made of. Ask where they think the material came from.
flow.say: Pick one thing. What is it made of? Where do you think that material first came from?
flow.kid: Pick one object. What is it made of? Where did it first come from?

ask.q: Where do you think the material first came from?
good: Oil from deep in the ground.

flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child chooses a different object and presents their circle to the others. Good objects: a steel katori (iron ore), a cotton shirt (cotton plant), a plastic bottle (oil or gas), a pencil (wood and graphite).
flow.context: This is the first step of Follow a Thing. You choose the object and guess its source.

flow.do: Draw four boxes in a circle: source, making, use and after. Write or draw what you know for each. Ask a grown-up where the object was bought. Ask how long it has been used. Ask what will happen to it when it is finished.
flow.say: Draw a circle of four boxes. Fill in what you know. Ask a grown-up what you do not know.
flow.kid: Draw four boxes in a circle. Fill in what you know.
flow.parent: Help your child find facts. If you do not know, say so. 'Not known' is a good answer.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the life of the object.

flow.do: Under each box, write what that stage uses up, such as energy, water, land or time. Circle the stage that you think uses most.
flow.say: What does each stage use up? Energy? Water? Land? Which stage do you think uses the most?
flow.kid: Write what each stage uses up. Circle the biggest.

ask.q: Which stage do you think uses the most?
good: Use, because it goes on for years.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer. For a steel katori, making uses a lot of energy, but a katori lasts for decades. A plastic bag is used for a few minutes, and then stays as waste for a very long time.
flow.context: In this step, you think about the cost of each stage.

flow.do: Write three questions you cannot yet answer about the life of your object. Choose one you could find out, and say how.
flow.say: What three questions do you have that you cannot answer? How could you find out one of them?
flow.kid: Write three questions you cannot answer yet.

check.q: Which is a good question about an object's whole life?
options: How much energy does it take to make, and how many times can it be used?
What colour is it?
Is it nice?
check.why: A good question about a whole life is one that can be measured or looked up, and it covers a stage of the life. The colour of an object, and whether it is nice, are about the object, not its life.

flow.context: In this step, you write the open questions. Knowing what we do not know is part of the science.

activities.title: Ask a Grandparent: what did people use before plastic?

materials.item: a grandparent, an older neighbour or an older relative, in person or on the phone
paper and a pencil to write down their answers
a camera or a phone, if they allow photos

schedule.what: Interview an older person. Write down five old materials and their jobs. Compare them with what we use now.

activities.record: A table with five rows, one for each material the older person mentions: the old material, the job, what it was good at, what it was bad at and what we use now.
activities.context: In this activity, you interview an older person about the materials they used when they were young, and you compare their choices with the ones we make today.

setup.art: A child sitting with a grandmother on a verandah, writing in a notebook while she holds a brass pot and a banana leaf.
setup.caption: 1. Sit with an older person and ask about their childhood.

setup.art: A table on paper with five rows and five columns: old material, job, good at, bad at, what we use now.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in the table for five materials.

flow.do: Ask your child to write five questions for an older person. Suggestions: what did you drink from, eat from, carry shopping in, write on and wrap things in when you were young?
flow.say: Write five questions for a grandparent about the things they used when they were young. What did they drink from? What did they carry things in?
flow.kid: Write five questions for an older person.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child writes their own questions. Then they take turns to ask them on one call, or each child interviews a different person and they share what they heard. Choose someone your child feels easy with. Phone calls are fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask a Grandparent. You prepare your questions.

flow.do: Interview the older person. Write down each material, its job and what they liked or disliked about it. Ask them what happened to the thing when it was done.
flow.say: Ask your questions. Write down each material, its job, and what they liked and disliked. Ask what happened to it afterwards.
flow.kid: Ask your questions. Write down the answers.

ask.q: What did people do with a thing when it was finished?

flow.parent: Expect banana leaf and areca leaf plates, brass and copper vessels, clay pots, coir and jute, cloth bags, glass bottles returned to the shop, and newspaper to wrap things. If they say something surprising, ask why.
flow.context: In this step, you talk and listen. The older person is the expert.

flow.do: Fill in the table. For each old material, write what we use now. Ask: is the new choice better, worse or just different? Why?
flow.say: For each old material, write what we use now. Is the new choice better, worse or different?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Compare old and new.

check.q: An older person says banana leaf plates were used because they cost nothing and rotted afterwards. Which words describe the leaf plates?
options: The leaf was cheap, light, and biodegradable
The leaf was strong and lasted for years
The leaf was a made material
check.why: A leaf plate costs little, is light and rots after use. It does not last for years, and it is not made in a factory. Choosing 'lasted for years' mixes up leaf plates with steel plates.

flow.context: In this step, you compare old and new choices fairly.

activities.title: Mend It: three ways to fix a torn paper strip

materials.item: 10 strips of newspaper, each 2 centimetres wide and 25 centimetres long
scissors used by a grown-up, wide sticky tape, thread and a needle with a blunt tip
a spoonful of flour paste and a small scrap of paper for the patch
a bucket or a mug with a handle and a loop of string, to hang from the strip
a jug or bottle of water and a measuring cup or a glass, to measure the water added
2 pencils or sticks, and the backs of two chairs or two piles of books to hang the strips from

schedule.what: Cut a slit 1 centimetre long in each of four paper strips. Mend three of them in three ways and leave one unmended. Then load each strip with water until it tears. Compare.

activities.record: A table with four rows: unmended, tape, paste patch and stitched. For each, the water in millilitres that the strip held before it tore (one millilitre weighs about one gram). A note on which mend was strongest and which was easiest.
activities.context: In this activity, you tear strips of paper, mend them in three different ways and test which mend is strongest. This is about repair, the third step in reduce, reuse, repair and recycle.

setup.art: Four paper strips with a cut halfway across the edge, one left plain, one with tape, one with a paste patch and one with stitches.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a 1 centimetre slit into each strip. Mend three of them in different ways.

setup.art: A strip hung from a pencil, with a bucket hanging from the bottom and a hand pouring water from a jug.
setup.caption: 2. Hang each strip. Pour water slowly into the bucket until it tears.

flow.do: Show your child the strips and the mending materials. Ask for a guess and a reason about which mend will hold the most.
flow.say: We will mend three strips three ways. One has tape. One has a paste patch. One has stitches. Which will hold the most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three mends. Which holds the most? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that mend will hold the most?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write each guess and its reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mend It. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Take 4 strips, each 2 centimetres wide. In the edge of each strip, cut a slit 1 centimetre long, which is halfway across. 2. Leave one strip unmended. 3. Put a strip of tape over the slit on the second strip. 4. Stick a paste patch over the slit on the third. 5. Sew three stitches across the slit on the fourth strip. Let the paste patch dry for 10 minutes.
flow.say: Cut a slit in each strip. Leave one alone. Mend one with tape, one with a paste patch and one with stitches. Wait ten minutes for the paste to dry.
flow.kid: Cut slits. Mend three strips three ways. Leave one.
flow.parent: A slit is a small crack. A mend can spread the load round it. Use the same size of tape, patch and number of stitches for each. Keep the mended area the same size.
flow.context: In this step, you cut and mend. The slit is a crack, which makes a strip weaker.

flow.do: Fold 2 centimetres at the top end of the strip over a pencil and tape it down well with wide tape. Do the same at the bottom end over a second pencil, and tie a string from that pencil to the bucket. Rest the top pencil across the backs of two chairs. Pour water slowly into the bucket until the strip tears. Measure the water in the bucket. Test the unmended strip too.
flow.say: Hang each strip. Pour water slowly into the bucket. Stop when it tears. Measure the water.
flow.kid: Hang a strip. Pour water slowly. Measure the water when it tears.
flow.parent: Pour at the same speed each time, and keep feet clear: the bucket will drop. Newspaper is stronger than it looks; a strip this size typically holds a kilogram or more, so use a bucket and be ready to pour for a while. If the strip tears at the tape and not at the slit, write that down: the mend was stronger than the paper. If every strip holds too much, make the slit longer, up to 1.5 centimetres. Do two strips of each kind if you have time. The unmended strip with a slit is your base number to beat. With 2 to 4 children, one pours, one watches the strip, one measures and one writes; swap for each strip.
flow.context: In this step, you test each mend. Pour the water slowly.

flow.do: Write the numbers in the table. Which mend held the most? Which was easiest to do? Which would you choose, and why?
flow.say: Which mend held the most? Which was easiest? Which would you choose?
flow.kid: Write the results. Which mend would you choose?

check.q: The stitched strip held 120 millilitres of water and the taped strip held 90. The unmended strip held 60. What does this tell you?
options: Both mends helped, and stitching helped more in this test
The tape made it weaker
The mend did nothing
check.why: Both mended strips held more than the unmended one. Stitches held more than tape. But one test cannot be sure of a small difference, so it is worth repeating. Choosing 'the tape made it weaker' reads the numbers the wrong way round.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the mends.

activities.title: Two Desks: one school in Chennai, one in Leh

materials.item: paper and a pencil to draw the tables
the Decision Matrix from Score the Cup, if you did it

schedule.what: List what a school desk needs. Score three materials for Chennai and for Leh. See whether the winner changes.

activities.record: Two decision matrices on paper, one for a school desk in Chennai and one for a school desk in Leh, with weights, scores and totals, and a sentence saying why the winner changed.
activities.context: In this activity, you choose materials for a school desk in two very different places, and see whether the same desk is the best in both.

setup.art: A school desk in a hot, humid classroom in Chennai with a ceiling fan, and another school desk in a cold classroom in Leh with a stove.
setup.caption: 1. Imagine two classrooms, one in Chennai and one in Leh.

setup.art: Two tables on paper side by side, with materials down the side and needs across the top.
setup.caption: 2. Make a decision matrix for each place.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what a school desk needs to do. Write a list of five needs. Possible needs are: not too heavy, comfortable to touch, strong, cheap, and not too easily damaged by damp.
flow.say: What does a school desk need to do? Write five needs. Which three matter most?
flow.kid: List five needs of a school desk. Choose the top three.

ask.q: Which needs matter most? Why?
good: Strong, because children climb on desks.
Cheap, because a school has many desks.
Comfortable, because children sit all day.

flow.context: This is the first step of Two Desks. You list the needs.

flow.do: Choose three materials for the desk top: wood, steel and hard plastic. Write what you know of each. How does it feel in the cold? How does it handle damp? How heavy and how costly is it?
flow.say: Pick three materials: wood, steel and hard plastic. What do you know about each one? How does each feel in the cold?
flow.kid: Pick three materials. Write what you know of each.
flow.parent: Hints: steel feels cold because it draws heat from your hand quickly. Wood feels warmer. Wood can swell in damp. Steel rusts in a damp climate. Plastic can crack in strong cold and sun.
flow.context: In this step, you gather what you know about three materials.

flow.do: Make a decision matrix for Chennai. Give weights and scores. Add up. Then make a second matrix for Leh, with different weights. Compare the winners.
flow.say: Make a table for Chennai. Make a second table for Leh. Change the weights. Do the winners match?
flow.kid: Make two tables. Compare the winners.
flow.parent: Look for the effect of place. In Leh, the cold feel matters. In Chennai, the damp and heat matter. There may be a different winner for each town. If not, discuss why.
flow.context: In this step, you score the three materials twice, once for each place.

flow.do: Ask your child to write one sentence that says why the best desk is different in the two places. Ask what a school in Kolkata might choose.
flow.say: Why is the best desk different in the two places? What would a school in Kolkata choose?
flow.kid: Write why the best desk differs. What about Kolkata?

check.q: Why might the best material for a desk be different in Chennai and in Leh?
options: The weather and what matters most are different in the two places
Chennai children are heavier
Steel is only made in Leh
check.why: The place changes which needs matter most, such as damp or cold. That changes the scores and the best choice. The other answers have no link to the materials.

flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found.

projects.title: Recycled Paper: make new paper from old paper

materials.item: about 6 sheets of old newspaper or used paper without glossy print
a big bowl and water, and a wide basin or tub for dipping the mesh
a masher such as a potato masher, or a blender used by a grown-up
a fine mesh, such as a piece of mosquito net, a net curtain or thin old cotton cloth, over a large sieve or stretched on a frame. A kitchen sieve with fine holes also works
an old towel or cloth, a few heavy books and a tray
a ruler, scissors used by a grown-up and a pencil
2 pencils or sticks, wide sticky tape, a bucket or mug with a handle, string, and a jug of water, to test the strips

schedule.what: Tear the paper into small bits and soak it in water.
Mash the soaked paper into pulp. Scoop it on the mesh, press out the water and leave the sheet to dry.
Peel off the new sheet and test strips of it against strips of newspaper.

projects.record: Photographs or drawings of each stage. The water in millilitres that strips of new paper and old newspaper held. A note on how the new sheet looks and feels compared with the old paper.
projects.context: In this project, you break old paper back into fibres and make a new sheet of paper from them. You test it against the old paper, and find out why recycling can make paper weaker.

setup.art: Torn bits of newspaper soaking in a bowl of water overnight.
setup.caption: 1. Tear the paper into small bits and soak it overnight.

setup.art: A child mashing the soaked paper with a potato masher in a bowl of water until it becomes a grey pulp.
setup.caption: 2. Mash the soaked paper into pulp.

setup.art: A mesh frame being lifted out of the bowl with a thin layer of pulp on it, and a hand pressing out water with a towel.
setup.caption: 3. Scoop the pulp on a mesh and press out the water.

setup.art: A new grey sheet of paper drying on a towel beside a pile of books.
setup.caption: 4. Press the sheet and let it dry.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how the new paper will compare with the old. Then tear the paper into pieces about the size of a thumbnail. Put them in the bowl. Cover them with water and leave them overnight.
flow.say: We will make new paper from old paper. Will it be as strong? Will it look the same? Why do you think so? Tear the paper into small bits and soak them overnight.
flow.kid: Tear the paper into small bits. Soak them overnight. Guess how strong the new paper will be.

ask.q: Will the new paper be as strong as the old paper? Why?
good: Yes, it is the same stuff.
It will be stronger because it is thicker.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Remove glossy, shiny or glued paper, since it does not turn into pulp well. Do not tip pulp down the sink, because it clogs the drain.
flow.context: This is the first step of Recycled Paper. You tear and soak the old paper, and guess.

flow.do: Day 2. Pour off most of the water. Mash the soaked paper with the masher until it is a smooth grey pulp. A grown-up can use a blender with the lid on and a little water.
flow.say: Mash the soaked paper into pulp. Keep going until it looks like thick porridge with no lumps.
flow.kid: Mash the wet paper into smooth pulp.
flow.parent: A blender makes shorter fibres than hand mashing. Short fibres make weaker paper. This is a way to see why recycled paper is weaker. Only a grown-up runs the blender: unplug it before touching the jug, and keep fingers away from the blades.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the paper back into fibres. This is how recycling works.

flow.do: Fill a tray with water. Stir in two big spoons of pulp. Slide the mesh under the water and lift it slowly, so a thin layer of pulp lies on it. Let the water drain. Press the layer with a towel to take up more water. Turn the mesh over on a clean towel and peel the mesh off. Cover the sheet with a second towel and put heavy books on top for an hour.
flow.say: Slide the mesh under the pulp. Lift slowly. Let the water drip. Press with a towel. Turn the sheet onto a towel. Put books on top.
flow.kid: Scoop the pulp on the mesh. Press out the water. Stack books on top.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, each child makes a sheet. One pulps, one dips, one presses. Swap. Compare each sheet. The first sheet may be lumpy or too thin. Try again with more or less pulp. Make 2 or 3 sheets if you can. Use a clean pencil to write the amount of pulp on the towel.
flow.context: In this step, you make the sheet. The first sheet is often uneven. Try more than one.

flow.do: Remove the books and leave the sheet to dry on the towel in a warm, airy place for a day or two. Do not peel it while damp.
flow.say: Leave the sheet to dry for a day or two. Do not peel it until it is dry.
flow.kid: Leave the sheet to dry.
flow.parent: A sheet can take two or three days to dry in damp weather. If the weather is humid, put the sheet near a fan. A sheet that is still damp will tear when peeled.
flow.context: In this step, you wait. The sheet dries and the fibres lock together as the water leaves.

flow.do: Day 3. Peel off the dry sheet. Cut a strip 2 centimetres wide. Cut a strip of the same size from the old newspaper. Test one strip at a time. Fold the top end of the strip over a pencil and tape it down. Fold the bottom end over a second pencil in the same way, and tie a string from that pencil to the bucket. Rest the top pencil across the backs of two chairs. Pour water slowly into the bucket until the strip tears. Measure the water. Compare the two strips. Look at the torn edges.
flow.say: Cut a strip of new paper and a strip of old paper, both the same width. Pour water slowly into a bucket until each tears. Which held more?
flow.kid: Test a strip of new paper and a strip of old. Compare.

ask.q: Which strip held more water before it tore? Why do you think so?
good: The old paper, because the fibres are longer.
The new paper, because it is thicker.

flow.parent: The new sheet is thicker and lumpier. It is usually weaker than newspaper because the fibres are shorter, but it may hold more or less, and either is a good result. A thin sheet may tear at the tape; put the tape over a wide fold. The point is to compare and talk about why.

check.q: Why is recycled paper usually weaker than new paper?
options: The fibres are broken and shorter each time paper is recycled
Recycled paper has no fibres
Recycled paper is wetter
check.why: Each time paper is pulped and remade, the fibres get shorter and fewer. Short fibres make fewer links, so the paper is weaker. Picking 'no fibres' mixes up recycled paper with plastic.

flow.context: In this step, you test the new paper against the old.

challenges.title: Leaf Bowl: hold 100 millilitres for ten minutes with nothing but leaves
challenges.problem: Make a bowl from leaves and small sticks only, with no plastic and no glue, that holds 100 millilitres of water for ten minutes without dripping onto the napkin below.
constraints: Use only leaves, thin sticks or toothpicks and string made of natural fibre. No plastic, no glue and no tape.
The bowl must hold 100 millilitres of water for ten minutes.
The napkin below must stay dry.
Write down every try, even the ones that leak.
materials: large leaves such as banana, areca or teak leaves from a vegetable seller or a tree nearby
a measuring cup or a medicine cup marked in millilitres
a paper napkin, a plate and a clock
general: Fold a large leaf into the shape of a cup, and pin the corners with toothpicks.
Use two leaves, one on top of the other, with the veins at right angles to each other.
Press the folds sharply so water cannot run along them.
creative: Stitch a leaf bowl with fibre, like traditional leaf bowls in many parts of India.
Make a bowl from a sheet of a large dried leaf, and then fix the edges with thread.
Make a stand from sticks so that the bowl sits flat.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your bowl. Build it and test it with 100 millilitres of water for ten minutes. If it leaks, change one thing, such as the fold, and test again. Which design worked best? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about making a useful thing from materials that rot. You build a bowl from leaves and test whether it holds water.

setup.art: Three sketches of leaf bowls on paper: a folded cup, a double-leaf bowl and a stitched bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch two or three leaf bowl designs.

setup.art: A child folding a banana leaf into a cup and pinning its corners with toothpicks.
setup.caption: 2. Build your bowl.

setup.art: A leaf bowl on a paper napkin with a measuring cup pouring water into it, and a clock beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Pour in 100 millilitres of water and time ten minutes.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to sketch two or three bowl designs. Ask why a leaf might hold water.
flow.say: You have only leaves and sticks. How could you make a bowl? Draw two or three ideas first.
flow.kid: Sketch two or three leaf bowl ideas.

ask.q: Why might a leaf hold water at all?
good: The surface is smooth and waxy.
Water does not soak into it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Bowl challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build your first bowl. Fold the leaf so that the folds are tight and the corners are held by toothpicks. Place the bowl on a napkin on a plate. Pour in 100 millilitres of water slowly, and start the clock.
flow.say: Build your bowl. Fold tightly. Pin the corners. Pour in water slowly. Start the clock.
flow.kid: Build a bowl. Pour in 100 millilitres. Start the clock.
flow.parent: If you cannot find a large leaf, use a big sheet of kitchen foil as a last resort, and talk about why it is a poorer choice, because foil does not rot. Where the toothpick goes through the leaf, water may seep out. Toothpicks have sharp points: push them in away from your fingers, and have a grown-up nearby.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test your first bowl.

flow.do: Check the napkin after one minute and after ten minutes. Where did it leak? Change one thing. Test again with a fresh napkin.
flow.say: Look at the napkin. Where did the water come out? Change one thing and test again.
flow.kid: Check the napkin. Change one thing. Test again.
flow.parent: Leaks are most often at the pin holes and at sharp folds. A double layer of leaf, or pins placed high above the water line, usually helps.
flow.context: In this step, you find the leaks and improve the bowl.

flow.do: Compare your tries. Which design was best? Ask: what is the catch of a leaf bowl compared with a steel bowl?
flow.say: Which design held water best? What is the catch of a leaf bowl compared with a steel bowl?
flow.kid: Compare your tries. What is the catch of a leaf bowl?

check.q: A leaf bowl held water for ten minutes. A steel bowl would last for years. What is one fair trade-off?
options: The leaf bowl rots and leaves no waste but cannot be used again, and the steel bowl lasts but must be washed
The leaf bowl is stronger
The steel bowl rots
check.why: Each choice gives up something. The leaf bowl cannot be used again, but it leaves no waste and needs no washing. The steel bowl must be washed, but it can be used for years. Saying one is stronger or better in every way misses the trade-off.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your designs and look at the trade-off.

challenges.title: The Zero-Bin Day: one day of everything we throw away
challenges.problem: For one whole day, keep everything your family would throw away in a basket. At the end of the day, sort it, and find three ways to throw away less tomorrow.
constraints: Keep everything, including food scraps, packaging and paper, in a basket or a bucket, except things that are unsafe or very dirty.
Do not hide or sneak anything out.
Sort everything at the end of the day into rots, can be reused or mended, can be remade, and is hard to deal with.
Use gloves or a spoon to handle the rubbish, and wash your hands.
materials: a big basket or bucket and a few trays or bowls for sorting
paper and a pencil to count and write
general: Count how many pieces of packaging there are, and which are plastic.
Find three things that could be avoided by choosing a different product.
Find one thing that could have been mended or reused.
creative: Lift the basket to feel how heavy it is, and draw how the pile might look after a week or a year.
Make a poster of what your family could do instead, with pictures.
Find a use for one thing from the basket, such as a jar, a tin or a cloth.
challenges.your_turn: Count what you threw away in a day. Sort it into four trays. Choose three things to change tomorrow. At the end of the next day, count again. Did the pile get smaller? Which changes were easy and which were hard? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a challenge about the whole life of the things we use. You find out what your family throws away in one day, and you try to reduce it.

setup.art: A basket in a kitchen with a label that says Today's rubbish, and a child dropping a wrapper into it.
setup.caption: 1. Keep everything in a basket for the day.

setup.art: Four trays on a table labelled Rots, Reuse or mend, Remade and Hard to deal with, with a child sorting items into them.
setup.caption: 2. At the end of the day, sort what is in the basket.

setup.art: A table on paper with a column for each tray and a tally of marks, beside a list of three changes.
setup.caption: 3. Count, and choose three changes.

flow.do: In the morning, put out the basket and explain the rules. Ask your child how big the pile will be by evening.
flow.say: All day, we keep what we would throw away in this basket. How big do you think the pile will be by the evening? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put out the basket. Guess how big the pile will be.

ask.q: How big will the pile be by the evening?
good: It will not fit in the basket.

flow.parent: Do not include dirty tissue, medicine packs or sharp things. Keep food scraps in a covered bowl so that they do not smell.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Zero-Bin Day. You set up the basket and guess.

flow.do: During the day, remind the family to put things in the basket. Count how many times you remember.
flow.say: Remember to put things in the basket. How many times did you remember?
flow.kid: Remind everyone to use the basket.
flow.parent: Most families find that they throw away much more than they expected. That is the result.
flow.context: In this step, the day goes by and the basket fills.

flow.do: At the end of the day, put on gloves. Sort everything into four trays: rots, reuse or mend, remade, and hard to deal with. Count the items in each tray.
flow.say: Sort everything into four trays. Count each tray. Which tray has the most?
flow.kid: Sort into four trays. Count each tray.

ask.q: Which tray has the most? Which has the least?
good: Hard to deal with had a surprising amount.

check.q: A paper cup lined with plastic goes in which tray?
options: Hard to deal with, because the paper and the plastic are stuck together
Rots, because paper rots
Remade, because all paper is remade
check.why: The paper rots but the thin plastic layer does not, and the two cannot easily be separated. Choosing 'rots' looks only at the paper.

flow.context: In this step, you sort and count, to see what the pile is made of.

flow.do: Choose three changes for tomorrow. Write each as a promise, such as 'we will carry a steel bottle'. Ask: which change will save the most? Which is the easiest?
flow.say: Choose three changes. Which will save the most? Which is the easiest?
flow.kid: Choose three changes. Write them as promises.
flow.parent: Remember the order: reduce first, then reuse, repair and recycle last.
flow.context: In this step, you choose your changes, using reduce, reuse, repair and recycle in order.

flow.do: Next evening, count again. Compare the two counts. Talk about what was easy and what was hard.
flow.say: Count again tomorrow. Is the pile smaller? What was easy? What was hard?
flow.kid: Count again tomorrow. Is the pile smaller?
flow.parent: A smaller pile is a good result. A pile that is the same is also a good result, because you found out what is hard to change.
flow.context: In this step, you check whether the changes worked.

items.p: Which sentence best describes a trade-off?
opts: Getting more of one good thing means giving up some of another
Choosing the cheapest thing every time
Having two good materials and using both
Finding the one best material for every job
items.why: A trade-off means that gaining something costs you something else. A thicker steel plate is stronger but heavier. Picking 'the one best material' usually means thinking one material can win on every need.

items.p: A strong material is the best material for every job.
items.why: False. A strong material may be too heavy, too costly or too hard to shape for a given job. A school bag strap of steel cable would be strong and useless.

items.p: A table that scores materials against the needs of a job is called a decision ____.
items.why: A decision matrix puts the materials down the side and the needs along the top, with scores and weights in the boxes.

items.p: Is each of these a composite, or not?
items: Bone, made of hard mineral and soft protein
items.a: see items
items.why: A composite is two or more different materials joined, so each does part of the job. A steel spoon is an alloy and a glass tumbler is mostly one material, so neither is a composite.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: A thin thread that carries the pull
The material that holds the fibres and shares the load
A metal mixed with other atoms
A source that can grow back in a lifetime
A pit where rubbish is buried
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each word names one idea: the thread, the glue, the mixed metal, the source that can come back and the place where rubbish goes.

items.p: In a bar of paper layers glued with paste, which part is the matrix?
opts: The water poured in the cup
items.why: The matrix is the material that holds the fibres and shares the load. In the paper and paste bar, the paste is the matrix and the paper is the fibre.
items.context: This question is about the Paper and Paste experiment. You make four kinds of bar from newspaper and flour paste, dry them, and test how much water each holds in a hanging cup.

items.p: Put the stages of a thing's whole life in order.
items: Source: where the material comes from
Making: it is made into a thing
After: it rots, rusts, is remade or stays
items.a: order shown
items.why: The material has to come from somewhere first. Then it is made into a thing. Then the thing is used. Only after that does it end up somewhere.

items.p: A banana peel is left in damp soil for two weeks. What will most likely happen to it?
opts: It rots, because bacteria and fungi break the peel down
items.why: A banana peel comes from a plant, and living things such as bacteria and fungi break plant material down. Rust belongs to iron, not to peel.

items.p: A plastic tumbler costs 20 rupees and cracks after 2 years. A steel tumbler costs 120 rupees and lasts 20 years. Explain which costs less for each year.
items.a: The plastic tumbler costs 20 divided by 2, which is 10 rupees a year. The steel tumbler costs 120 divided by 20, which is 6 rupees a year. So the steel tumbler costs less for each year, even though it costs more at the shop.
items.why: Dividing the price by the number of years gives a fair way to compare a cheap thing that breaks with a dear thing that lasts.

items.p: What is brass?
opts: An alloy of copper and zinc
items.why: Brass is copper mixed with zinc. The zinc atoms are a different size, so they stop layers of copper atoms from sliding, and the brass is harder than copper.

items.p: Steel is a pure metal with no other atoms in it.
items.why: False. Steel is iron mixed with a small amount of carbon. It is an alloy, and the carbon makes it harder than pure iron.

items.p: The four steps, in order, are reduce, reuse, ____ and recycle.
items.why: Reduce means to make and buy less. Reuse means to use a thing again. Repair means to mend it. Recycle, the last step, means to break it down and make something new.

items.p: Where does each thing most likely end up? Does it rot, or can it be remade?
items.a: see items
items.why: Plant materials rot, because living things can break them down. Steel, glass and aluminium can be melted and made again.

items.p: Look at the table. How many times more water did the layered bar C hold than the plain paste bar A?
items.why: Bar C held 150 millilitres and bar A held 30. 150 divided by 30 is 5. Picking 120 means taking away instead of dividing.
items.context: This question is about the Paper and Paste experiment. You make four kinds of bar from newspaper and flour paste, dry them, and test how much water each holds in a hanging cup.

chart.title: Made-up results: water held before the bar snapped or sank 2 centimetres
rows: Four paper layers glued with paste

items.p: Draw the life of a cotton shirt in four boxes in a circle, from source to after. Write one thing in each box.
items.a: Source: a cotton field. Making: a mill and a tailor. Use: worn and washed many times. After: mended, passed on, or rotting in soil. Arrows go round the circle.
items.why: A life cycle has four stages. Drawing them as a circle shows that what comes after can lead back to a source.
items.art: A circle of four boxes joined by arrows, with a cotton field, a loom, a child wearing a shirt and a heap of cloth in soil.

items.p: A village needs a footbridge over a stream. People have different ideas.

views.says: Make a bamboo bridge. Bamboo grows back quickly and costs little.
Make a steel bridge. Steel is strong and will last for decades.
Lead the roots of a fig tree across the stream. It will be ready in many years, but it will mend itself.

items.ask: Whose idea would you choose? Give one reason. Say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer weighs the needs: how soon, how long, cost, what happens after. Bamboo is quick and cheap but rots in a few years. Steel lasts but needs paint and is hard to dispose of. Roots take longest but last longest and leave no waste. Each person is right about one need. A village could also choose two.
items.why: The best choice depends on what the village counts. A decision matrix shows how the weights decide.

items.p: A plastic tiffin box and a steel tiffin box both score 30 in a decision matrix. What is the best next step?
opts: Look at the weights and ask which need matters most for this job
items.why: A tie shows that the scores alone cannot settle the matter. The weights, which say what matters most, can. If the box is carried with curry, 'does not leak' gets a bigger weight.

items.p: A 600 rupee pair of shoes lasts 2 years. A 300 rupee pair lasts 6 months. Which costs less for each year?
opts: The 600 rupee pair, at 300 rupees a year
The 300 rupee pair, at 300 rupees a year
The 300 rupee pair, at 600 rupees a year
items.why: 600 divided by 2 years is 300 a year. 300 divided by half a year is 600 a year. So the dearer shoes cost less each year.

items.p: Every time paper is recycled, the fibres get longer and the paper gets stronger.
items.why: False. Each time paper is pulped and remade, the fibres get shorter and fewer, so the paper gets weaker.

items.p: A material made of fibres held by a matrix is called a ____.
items.why: A composite is made of two or more materials joined so that the result can do what neither could do alone.

items.p: For a steel pot, does making the walls thicker make each of these better or worse?
items: How fast the pot heats up
How well the pot keeps food hot
items.a: see items
items.why: Thicker steel gives more strength and long life, and holds more heat. It also adds weight and cost, and takes longer to heat. That is a trade-off.

items.p: Give two reasons why the best roof for a house in Cherrapunji might not be the best roof for a house in the Thar desert.
items.a: In Cherrapunji, the roof has to shed very heavy rain, so it must be sloped and must not rot in the damp. In the Thar desert, the roof has to keep out the midday heat, so it must be thick and made of a material that heats slowly. The place changes which needs matter most.
items.why: The same job can need different materials in different places, because the needs have different weights.

items.p: Match each place to a good reason for its choice.
pairs: A mud wall in the Thar desert
Thick walls heat slowly and keep the inside cool
Wood is not icy to sit on
A clay matka in a village home
Water seeps through the clay and cools the water inside
A steel bottle in a school bag
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each choice answers a need that the place makes important: heat, rain, cold, cooling and rough handling.

items.p: Why does stainless steel rust much less than ordinary steel?
opts: It has chromium mixed in, which forms a thin protective skin on the surface
It has no iron in it
items.why: Chromium atoms in stainless steel form a very thin invisible layer that protects the metal below. Stainless steel is still an alloy of iron.

items.p: Put these scraps in order, from rotting fastest to rotting slowest, in warm damp soil.
items.a: order shown
items.why: A banana peel is soft food for bacteria and fungi. Paper is made from plant fibres, but is drier and harder. Cotton is a tougher plant fibre and takes months. Plastic does not rot at all in a short time.

items.p: Draw a mud brick with straw in it, and show a crack starting from one side. Show where the crack stops, and say why.
items.a: A rectangle with straw lines through it. A crack starts at an edge and stops when it meets a straw fibre. The fibre carries the pull and stops the crack from running through.
items.why: In a composite, the fibres stop cracks from running straight through the matrix.
items.art: A cut-open mud brick with thin straw lines inside, and a crack starting from the left edge and ending at a straw fibre.

items.p: Aluminium can be melted and made into new things again and again with little loss of quality.
items.why: True. Aluminium is a metal, and its atoms stay the same when it is melted. Recycling it takes far less energy than making new aluminium from ore.

items.p: In the past, tests of asbestos asked, 'does it do the job?' What question was missing?
opts: What does it do to people's lungs years later?
items.why: A test answers only the question it asks. Asbestos did the job, but doctors found years later that its fibres could harm the lungs. This is why engineers look at the whole life.

items.p: Some campaigners want to ban all plastic. Others disagree.

views.says: Ban it. Plastic waste is in rivers and soil, and it lasts a very long time.
Plastic is in syringes, blood bags and helmets. We cannot do without it everywhere.
Use plastic only where nothing else will do, and design everything to be reused or remade.

items.ask: Whose idea would you choose? Give one reason. Say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer weighs the harm against the benefits. The campaigner is right that single-use plastic is a huge problem. The doctor is right that some uses save lives. The designer's idea tries to keep what is useful and remove the harm.
items.why: Banning all or keeping all are both too simple. Looking at the job, the whole life and the alternatives helps to decide.

items.p: In reinforced concrete, what do the steel bars do?
opts: They carry the pulling, which concrete is weak at
items.why: Concrete is strong when squeezed but weak when pulled. The steel bars carry the pull. This is a composite at work.

items.p: A material that can be broken down by bacteria and fungi is called ____.
items.why: Biodegradable materials return to the soil. A banana peel is one, and a plastic bag is not.

items.p: Explain in your own words why a bar made of weak paper and weak paste can be strong.
items.a: The paste is brittle and snaps, and the paper bends. Together the paste holds the paper layers so they cannot slide, and the paper stops cracks from running through the paste. Each part does the job the other cannot do.
items.why: A composite works because each material covers the other's weakness.
items.context: This question is about the Paper and Paste experiment. You make four kinds of bar from newspaper and flour paste, dry them, and test how much water each holds in a hanging cup.

items.p: After two weeks, the cotton cloth in the Burial Test looks hardly changed. Which claim is fair?
opts: It changed little in two weeks, and may take months to rot
Cotton rots faster than banana peel
items.why: Two weeks is a short time. A test shows what happened in that time only. Cotton comes from a plant and can rot, but much more slowly than a peel.
items.context: This question is about the Burial Test. You bury six scraps in damp soil for two weeks and score what has changed.

items.p: A cloth bag costs 40 rupees. A plastic bag costs 2 rupees and is used once. After how many uses does the cloth bag cost less per use than buying a new plastic bag each time?
items.why: 40 divided by 2 is 20. After 20 uses the cloth bag has cost the same as 20 plastic bags. After that, each use is cheaper.

items.p: A cloth bag at 40 rupees breaks even with 2 rupee plastic bags after ____ uses.
items.why: 40 divided by 2 is 20. After 20 uses, the cloth bag has paid for itself.

items.p: Some people say 'natural means harmless'. Give one example that shows this is not always true.
items.a: Asbestos is a natural mineral, but its tiny fibres can harm the lungs. Some natural plants are poisonous. A material is harmless or harmful because of what it does, not because it is natural.
items.why: Natural and harmless are different ideas. The test of a material is what it does to bodies and places.

items.p: A small town on a river must choose how to build a new bridge. They disagree.

views.says: Build a steel bridge. It is quick, and we need it for next year's market.
Build a concrete bridge. It lasts, and children can cross it for fifty years.
Plant fig trees and lead the roots across. It takes many years, but costs little and mends itself.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Give one reason. Say what another person has right.
items.a: A good answer uses a decision matrix: time, cost, life, repair and what happens after. The shopkeeper is right about speed. The teacher is right about life and strength. The farmer is right about repair and low cost over time. A town could build a quick bridge now and start a second slow one.
items.why: The best choice depends on how much weight we give to speed, cost over time, repair and waste.

items.p: Which is the best sign that an old tradition of using a material is wise?
opts: There is a reason we can test, such as water cooling in a clay pot
It is part of a festival
items.why: Old and popular do not make a belief true. A reason that can be tested does. Water seeping through a clay pot and cooling it can be measured.

items.p: A material that rots is always the better choice.
items.why: False. Some 'compostable' materials only break down in very hot industrial composters, and a thing made to rot may be used once and need a lot of land and water to grow. A thing used many times can be kinder.

items.p: Is each action reduce, reuse or repair?
items: Carrying your own steel bottle so you need no plastic one
Using a pickle jar to store rice
Saying no to a plastic bag you do not need
Giving old clothes to a younger cousin
Gluing the handle back on a broken cup
items.a: see items
items.why: Reduce means not making or buying in the first place. Reuse means using a thing again. Repair means mending it.

items.p: Match each material to what usually happens to it after use.
pairs: Iron nail left in damp air
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Plant materials rot, steel can be remade, iron rusts and most plastics stay a very long time.

items.p: Bone is hard, yet slightly bendy. Which explanation fits?
opts: It is a composite of hard mineral and soft protein
It is made of one kind of atom only
It is a kind of plastic
items.why: The mineral makes bone hard and the protein makes it tough, so a crack does not run straight through. This is how a composite works.

items.p: Draw the life of a plastic bottle in four boxes in a circle. Add a second arrow to show it being remade, and a third to show it staying in the ground.
items.a: Source: oil or gas from the ground. Making: a factory. Use: a drink, a few days. After: three arrows, one to a recycling plant and back to a new bottle, one to a landfill, and one to a river.
items.why: A life cycle can have different endings. The ending depends on who collects the bottle and what they do with it.
items.art: A circle of four boxes with a bottle, and three arrows leaving the last box to a recycling plant, a landfill and a river.

items.p: Titanium works inside the body because bone grows tightly onto it. What would you test before putting a new material inside a person?
items.a: I would test whether the body rejects it, whether it corrodes in body fluids, how strong it is, whether it wears into the surrounding bone, and how long it lasts. I would test in the laboratory first, then with careful trials. I would also watch for harm many years later.
items.why: A new material in the body must be tested for many needs and for the long term, since a test answers only the question it asks.

items.p: A cup is sold as 'compostable', but it only breaks down in very hot industrial composters. What happens to the cup in a family that has no such composter?
opts: The cup may stay for a long time, so the claim does not help them
The cup rots in their garden in a week
The cup is eaten by animals
The cup turns into soil in their kitchen
items.why: A claim about rotting depends on where it happens. A family without the right composter gets little benefit. It is important to ask 'where?' and 'how fast?'

items.p: Making a new aluminium can from ore takes far more ____ than making one from old cans.
items.why: Recycling aluminium needs only a small part of the energy of making it from ore. This is why aluminium is worth collecting.

items.p: The iron pillar of Delhi has hardly rusted in about 1,500 years. People give different reasons.

views.says: The iron has a lot of phosphorus. A thin skin formed on the surface and protected it.
Delhi is dry for most of the year. The place did much of the work.
We should also remember how people have touched and treated the pillar. We may not know the whole story.

items.ask: Whose idea do you find the most convincing? Give one reason. Say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer says that all three may be partly right. The skin on the surface and the dry weather can work together, and the history of care adds a third part. The honest answer is that the reasons are still debated.
items.why: This is a question where scientists still disagree. A good answer says what we know, what we do not, and how a test could help.

items.p: A test that asks only 'does it do the job?' can miss harm that appears many years later.
items.why: True. A test answers only the question it asks. Asbestos and lead did their jobs well, and the harm showed up years afterwards.

items.p: Choose a material for a school bag in Kochi in the monsoon. Give your needs, your weights and your choice, in a few lines.
items.a: Needs: waterproof (weight 3), light (weight 2), strong (weight 2), cheap (weight 1), and what happens after (weight 1). A coated nylon bag scores high for waterproof and light. A cotton bag scores low for waterproof. My choice: coated nylon, with the catch that it lasts a long time as waste, so I would use it for many years.
items.why: A good choice states the needs, the weights and the catch.

quiz.p: What does it mean to say that a choice is a trade-off?
opts: Getting more of one good thing costs you some of another
quiz.why: A trade-off means every choice gives up something. Picking 'one material wins' ignores the catch every material has.

quiz.p: A decision matrix gives two cups the same total. What helps most to decide?
opts: Checking which need matters most for the job
quiz.why: The weights say what matters most. When totals tie, the argument is really about the weights.

quiz.p: A bar of paper glued with paste holds far more than a bar of dried paste alone. What best explains it?
opts: The paper carries the pull and the paste holds the layers so they cannot slide
The paste is stronger than steel
quiz.why: In a composite, each material covers the other's weakness. The fibre carries the pull and the matrix holds it in place.

quiz.p: Why is bronze harder than pure copper?
opts: Tin atoms of a different size get in the way when layers of copper atoms try to slide
quiz.why: Atoms of a different size jam the layers. This is why alloys are harder than pure metals.

quiz.p: Which stage is not part of the whole life of a steel katori?
quiz.why: A katori's life is source, making, use and after. It never turns into a plant. It can be melted and made again.

quiz.p: A banana peel, a steel can and a plastic bag are left in damp soil for a long time. Which statement is most accurate?
opts: The peel rots, the can rusts or is remade, and the bag stays a very long time
All three rot at the same speed
quiz.why: Living things break down the peel. Iron in the can slowly rusts. Most plastics resist breaking down. These are different endings.

quiz.p: Shoes at 400 rupees last 2 years. Shoes at 150 rupees last 6 months. Which costs less for each year?
opts: The 400 rupee shoes, at 200 rupees a year
The 150 rupee shoes, at 150 rupees a year
The 150 rupee shoes, at 300 rupees a year
quiz.why: 400 divided by 2 is 200 a year. 150 divided by half a year is 300 a year. The dearer shoes cost less each year.

quiz.p: A test that shows a material did its job today proves it is safe for many years.
quiz.why: False. A test answers only the question it asks. Asbestos and lead did their jobs, and showed harm years later.

quiz.p: Which comes first when we try to throw away less?
quiz.why: The order is reduce, reuse, repair, recycle. Not making the thing in the first place saves the most.

quiz.p: Why does the best desk for Leh differ from the best desk for Chennai?
opts: The place changes which needs matter most, such as cold or damp
Steel cannot be made in Leh
Desks are only made in Chennai
quiz.why: The needs change with the place, so the scores and the best choice change.

quiz.p: Why is recycled paper often weaker than new paper?
opts: The fibres get shorter each time paper is pulped and remade
quiz.why: Short fibres make fewer links, so the paper is weaker.

quiz.p: What do the steel bars do in reinforced concrete?
opts: They carry the pull, which concrete is weak at
quiz.why: Concrete is strong when squeezed and weak when pulled. The bars carry the pull. It is a composite.

open_questions.q: Can we make a plastic that is strong when we need it and rots when we are finished, in any ordinary place?
open_questions.why_open: Some new plastics rot only in hot industrial composters. Scientists are still looking for ones that break down in soil, rivers and the sea without leaving tiny pieces.

open_questions.q: Why has the Iron Pillar of Delhi lasted so long without rusting?
open_questions.why_open: Several explanations may each be partly right, and scientists still debate how much each one matters.

open_questions.q: Can enzymes from bacteria and fungi clean up the plastic already in the ground?
open_questions.why_open: Enzymes work on some plastics in a laboratory, but nobody yet knows if they can work at the scale of a landfill or an ocean.

open_questions.q: How do we find out the long-term harm of a new material before it is used everywhere?
open_questions.why_open: Some harms, such as asbestos in the lungs, take many years to show. Scientists are still working out how to test for slow harm quickly.

open_questions.q: Could we grow materials, like a living root bridge, instead of making them in factories?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are growing packaging from fungus and building materials from bacteria, but nobody knows yet how strong, cheap and widely useful they can become.

open_questions.q: Is there an honest way to compare the costs of two materials when the costs fall on different people and different years?
open_questions.why_open: Economists and engineers use different methods and disagree about which costs to count and how much the future should matter.

If you could choose one material for a house in your town, which would it be, and what would you give up?
What did your grandparents use before plastic?
What can you reuse or mend at home this week?
Which would you rather have, a cheap thing that breaks soon or a dearer thing that lasts? Why?
Why do you think some things rot and others stay?
Where does your school bag end up when you are done with it?
What material would you invent, and what would it be good at?
How could we test an old way of doing something?
What would you want to know about a new material before we used it everywhere?

jokes.j: Why did the paper and the paste get along so well?
jokes.a: Together they held up under pressure.

jokes.j: Why did the steel tumbler get a gold star?
jokes.a: It never gave up, and it only needed a wash.

jokes.j: What did the banana peel say to the soil?
jokes.a: I'll be back, but as a different kind of banana.

jokes.j: Why did the plastic bag feel so lonely?
jokes.a: It was still around long after everyone else had gone.

jokes.j: Why was the mud brick so calm?
jokes.a: It had straw to lean on.

jokes.j: Why did the cloth bag win the argument?
jokes.a: It came back for twenty rounds.

jokes.j: What did the matrix say to the fibre?
Why did the decision matrix always bring a calculator?
jokes.a: It liked to weigh its options.

jokes.j: Why was the glass bottle the best at reusing?
jokes.a: It kept coming back for a refill.

jokes.j: Why did the clay kullad never complain?
jokes.a: It always returned to its roots.

maths.problem: A steel tumbler costs 120 rupees and lasts 20 years. A plastic tumbler costs 20 rupees and lasts 2 years. How much does each cost for each year? Which costs less each year, and by how much?
maths.answer: Steel: 6 rupees a year. Plastic: 10 rupees a year. The steel tumbler costs 4 rupees less each year.
maths.explain: 120 divided by 20 is 6. 20 divided by 2 is 10. 10 take away 6 is 4. So the steel tumbler costs 4 rupees less each year, even though it costs 6 times as much at the shop.
maths.context: In the Score the Cup activity, you find the price of each cup and how long it lasts, and work out the cost for each year.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the price by the years gives a fair way to compare a cheap thing that breaks soon with a dear thing that lasts.

maths.problem: In a decision matrix for a cup, the needs have weights: light 3, comfortable 1, does not leak 3, cost for each year 2 and what happens after 1. Steel scores 2, 3, 5, 4 and 4. Plastic scores 5, 4, 4, 3 and 1. Work out each total. Which wins? If the weight for what happens after goes up to 3, which wins now?
maths.answer: Steel 36, plastic 38, so plastic wins. With after at weight 3, steel is 44 and plastic is 40, so steel wins.
maths.explain: Steel: 2 times 3 is 6, 3 times 1 is 3, 5 times 3 is 15, 4 times 2 is 8, 4 times 1 is 4. Adding them one at a time gives 6, 9, 24, 32 and then 36. Plastic: 15, 4, 12, 6 and 1, which add up to 38. If the last weight is 3, steel gains 8 more to make 44 and plastic gains 2 more to make 40. The winner changed because what we care about changed.
maths.context: In the Score the Cup activity, you score four cups against five needs, multiply by weights and add the rows.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying each score by its weight and adding up lets you compare materials on many needs at once, and see how the winner changes when the weights change.

maths.problem: In made-up Paper and Paste results, bar A held 30 millilitres and bar C held 150 millilitres. How many times more did bar C hold? Bar B held 8 millilitres. How many times more did bar C hold than bar B? Give the second answer to the nearest whole number.
maths.answer: Bar C held 5 times as much as bar A and about 19 times as much as bar B.
maths.explain: 150 divided by 30 is 5. 150 divided by 8 is 18.75, which is about 19. So the glued layers held far more than either the paste alone or the loose paper stack.
maths.context: In the Paper and Paste experiment, you test bars made of paste, loose paper, glued paper layers and paste with fibres, by pouring water into a hanging cup.
maths.why_maths: A ratio says how many times stronger one bar is than another, which is a clearer way to see a composite's advantage than the two raw numbers.

maths.problem: Reports say that making a new aluminium can from ore uses about 100 units of energy, and making one from old cans uses about 5 units. If you have 100 units of energy, how many cans can you make from old cans? How many from ore?
maths.answer: 20 cans from old cans, and 1 can from ore.
maths.explain: 100 divided by 5 is 20. 100 divided by 100 is 1. So the same energy makes 20 times as many cans when they are made from old cans. The numbers are rough, and they differ in different studies, but the saving is big.
maths.context: This question is about the energy needed to recycle aluminium, which is why aluminium cans are worth collecting.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the energy by the energy per can shows how many cans each method makes, and why recycling some materials saves so much.

maths.problem: A cloth bag costs 40 rupees. A plastic bag costs 2 rupees and is used once. After how many uses has the cloth bag cost the same as buying plastic bags? After 50 uses, how many rupees has the cloth bag saved?
maths.answer: 20 uses. After 50 uses, the cloth bag has saved 60 rupees.
maths.explain: 40 divided by 2 is 20 plastic bags. After 50 uses, 50 plastic bags would cost 50 times 2, which is 100 rupees. The cloth bag cost 40. 100 take away 40 is 60 rupees saved.
maths.context: This question is about the choice between a cloth bag and plastic carry bags, which depends on how many times each is used.
maths.why_maths: Finding the break-even point tells you how long you must use a thing before it pays for itself.

maths.problem: A family uses 3 plastic carry bags a day. About how many bags is that in a year of 365 days? In ten years? Round 365 to 400 to estimate.
maths.answer: About 1,200 bags in a year, and about 12,000 in ten years. The exact answers are 1,095 and 10,950.
maths.explain: 3 times 400 is 1,200. Ten years is 12,000. The exact number is 3 times 365, which is 1,095, and then 10,950 for ten years. The estimate is a little high but close, and it is quick to work out in your head.
maths.context: This question is about the 'reduce' step, where you think about how many things a family throws away in a year.
maths.why_maths: Rounding makes big numbers easy to work with in your head, which helps to see how small habits add up.

maths.problem: In the Burial Test, 6 scraps were buried. 2 rotted a lot, 1 changed a little and 3 did not change. What fraction rotted a lot? What fraction changed at all?
maths.answer: One third rotted a lot, and one half changed at all.
maths.explain: 2 out of 6 is the same as 1 out of 3. The scraps that changed at all are 2 plus 1, which is 3 out of 6, or one half.
maths.context: In the Burial Test, you bury six scraps in damp soil for two weeks and score what has changed.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let you say how much of a group did something, and compare it with another group of a different size.

maths.problem: You bury the scraps on Monday 3 March. You look through the cups on day 7 and dig them out on day 14. What are the two dates? What day of the week is each?
maths.answer: Day 7 is Monday 10 March. Day 14 is Monday 17 March.
maths.explain: 7 days after 3 March is 10 March. 14 days after 3 March is 17 March. Seven days is exactly one week, so the day of the week stays Monday each time.
maths.context: In the Burial Test, you check the cups on day 7 and dig up the scraps on day 14.
maths.why_maths: Counting days on a calendar lets you plan checks at fair, equal gaps.

maths.problem: In this made-up example, a fig root is 4 centimetres across and gets 1 centimetre thicker every year. How thick is it after 15 years? In which year does it first pass 12 centimetres?
maths.answer: 19 centimetres after 15 years. It passes 12 centimetres in year 9.
maths.explain: 4 plus 15 is 19. To pass 12 centimetres, it needs more than 8 years of growth, so in year 9 it is 13 centimetres. The numbers are made up. Real roots grow at different speeds in different years.
maths.context: This question is about a living root bridge, where the roots get thicker each year. The growth rate is made up.
maths.why_maths: A steady growth each year is a pattern you can add up, which shows how a slow material becomes strong over time.

maths.problem: In this made-up example, bone is about two-thirds hard mineral and one-third soft protein. A piece of bone weighs 300 grams. How many grams are mineral? How many are protein?
maths.answer: 200 grams of mineral and 100 grams of protein.
maths.explain: One third of 300 is 100. Two thirds is 2 times 100, which is 200. So 200 grams are mineral and 100 grams are protein. The two add up to 300.
maths.context: This question is about bone as a composite of hard mineral and soft protein. The shares are rounded for this example.
maths.why_maths: Finding a fraction of a weight shows how much of each part there is in a composite.
