roots.context: In this unit you made bars from paper and paste, scored cups and followed things from the ground to the bin. This part asks what all of that tells us about materials, and about what we ourselves are made of.

deep_truth.truth: A strip of paper bends easily. A bar of dried paste snaps. Glue four layers of paper together with that paste, and the bar holds many times more than either one alone. The strength comes from how the parts are joined.
deep_truth.habit: We name what a thing is made of, 'it is paper' or 'it is paste', and think that tells us what it can do. But this leaves out how the parts are put together. The same ingredients, put together in two ways, can give two very different things.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Paper and Paste experiment, the plain paste bar and the loose paper stack each failed early. The paper glued with paste held far more. Your own numbers may be different, and you should write them just as they are.

three.who_am_i: Your bones are a composite of a hard mineral and a soft protein. The mineral alone would be brittle like chalk, and the protein alone would be bendy like rubber. Your bones work because the two are joined.
three.what_is_life: Where two fig roots touch, they can join and grow into one thicker root. A living root bridge is mended by the same roots that make it, and not by anything brought in from outside.
three.what_is_this_world: Mud with straw, steel in concrete, copper with tin: the world's most useful things are mixtures. What each mixture can do depends on how the parts are put together, as well as on the parts.

roots.thread: Every question in this unit came back to how things are joined. Paper and paste, straw and mud, copper and tin, and two fig roots are each more than their ingredients. What a thing is good for depends on how its parts are joined, where it is used and how many years it lasts. So knowing what a thing is made of is not enough. We also need to know how it is put together, where it is, and what becomes of it afterwards. Choosing a material is not like looking up a number in a table. It means looking at the whole picture.

teachings.link: A pot, a cup and a kullad are different shapes of one clay. When we choose a material, we choose the stuff. But what we make from it, and how we make it, decides what it is used for.

science.text: Composites such as reinforced concrete, wood, bone and fibreglass get their strength from how fibres and matrix share the load, and this has been measured many times.

There are several ideas about why the Iron Pillar of Delhi has hardly rusted, including the phosphorus in the iron, the dry climate and its history of care. Scientists still debate how much each one matters.
Nobody knows yet whether we can make strong, low-cost materials that also rot, or can be remade easily, anywhere.

other_view.view: Many materials engineers say that a composite's strength can be worked out with a rule, from the strengths of the parts and the way they share the load. So nothing new appears when the parts are joined. The strength was already there in the numbers for the fibre and the matrix, and the maths just adds it up. To them, the strength of a composite is not a mystery, but a result you can calculate.

practice.title: Braid and pull
practice.say: Take three loose threads or hair ties. Hold one thread at each end and pull gently. Notice how weak it is. Now braid the three together, and pull again. Feel how much stronger it is. Breathe in slowly and out slowly three times. Think of your family, or your friends, as threads. Each one is easy to bend, and together they hold.
practice.kid: Take three threads. Pull one. It is weak. Braid all three and pull. It is strong. Breathe three times.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat today, but not yet tried with a child. Paper and Paste: the flour paste is cold and needs no cooking, and a pinch of salt may slow mould. The bars need two full days to dry, and in very humid weather a fan or three to four days help. The plain paste bar is brittle and may break while it is peeled from the plastic. The steps say to record that as a result and use the spare bar. The test rig is two piles of books with a 12 centimetre gap, a paper cup on a thread and a slow stream of water, with the failure defined as a snap or a sag of 2 centimetres. The loose paper stack sags at once with only a few millilitres, and this is the expected result. The layered bar usually holds many times more, but real numbers will vary and that is fine. Burial Test: needs soil, which a flowerpot gives, and a shady balcony or windowsill. By day 14 the banana peel and the newspaper have usually changed a lot, while cotton often shows only a little change, and the plastic and foil show none. This is a real result and the step says so. Mould may appear, and the safety line says not to sniff it. Score the Cup uses hot drinking-temperature water poured by a grown-up, never boiling. Mend It uses a slit as a small crack and loads the strip with water in a bucket, because newspaper strips hold about a kilogram or more. Recycled Paper needs a grown-up for a blender, and its strips are loaded with water in a bucket. Mashing by hand also works and gives longer fibres. The Leaf Bowl needs large leaves from a vegetable seller, and foil is named as a last resort with the trade-off discussed. The spine is the Paper and Paste experiment, which starts in the first session (about 30 minutes) and is finished in the second session two days later (about 35 minutes), together with the explanations, Roots and quiz. Facts to check before release: the Brånemark dates and the rabbit studies, the Yoshida 2016 findings, the Iron Pillar's age and the competing explanations, the aluminium recycling energy figure, the phase-out year of leaded petrol in India, and the Upanishad and Kabir wording. The story's characters and the cost of a steel bridge are made up.
